chapters.title: The Competencies of a Business Analyst
The Strategic Context for Business Analysis

questions.stem: A retailer's board has approved a new strategy and a regulator has issued guidance that changes what the business must do. Before any change initiative is scoped, a business analyst is asked to check that the proposed changes fit this wider context. Which stage of the business change lifecycle is this?

options.text: Alignment
options.note: Alignment fits change initiatives to the external business environment, the enterprise architecture and the business strategy.

options.text: Definition
options.note: Definition follows alignment and analyses the business situation and requirements.

options.text: Design
options.note: Design follows definition and produces the design specification, development and testing.

options.text: Implementation
options.note: Implementation is the deployment of the agreed solution.

options.text: Realisation
options.note: Realisation is the post-implementation review of benefits.

options.text: Business case
options.note: The business case sits at the centre of the lifecycle rather than being one of its stages.

questions.explanation: Alignment is the stage that lines up proposed change with the external environment, the enterprise architecture and business strategy. Definition only begins once that context is set.

questions.stem: A business analyst is examining how a claims team works today and what the business needs from a new way of working, so that efficiency and effectiveness improve. Which lifecycle stage is this?

options.text: Definition
options.note: Definition analyses the business situation and the requirements in order to determine new ways of working that improve efficiency and effectiveness.

options.text: Alignment
options.note: Alignment comes earlier and concerns the external environment, enterprise architecture and business strategy.

options.text: Design
options.note: Design turns agreed requirements into a design specification.

options.text: Implementation
options.note: Implementation is the deployment of the agreed solution.

options.text: Realisation
options.note: Realisation is the review of benefits after deployment.

options.text: Feasibility assessment
options.note: Feasibility assessment is part of business case work, not a stage of the lifecycle.

questions.explanation: Analysing the current situation and shaping requirements into new ways of working is definition. Alignment has already set the strategic context by this point.

questions.stem: A bank has agreed its requirements. Work now moves to producing the design specification and then building the solution against it. Which lifecycle stage is under way?

options.text: Design
options.note: Design covers change design and development: the design specification and the build of the solution.

options.text: Definition
options.note: Definition produced the requirements and is complete before design begins.

options.text: Implementation
options.note: Implementation follows design and deploys the solution.

options.text: Realisation
options.note: Realisation follows deployment and reviews whether benefits were delivered.

options.text: Alignment
options.note: Alignment is the earliest stage and sets the strategic context.

options.text: Business case
options.note: The business case is the element at the centre of the lifecycle, not a stage.

questions.explanation: The design stage produces the design specification and covers development of the solution. Definition produced the requirements and is complete before design begins.

questions.stem: The new system has passed acceptance testing and is being rolled out branch by branch, with staff trained and customer records migrated as each branch goes live. Which lifecycle stage is this?

options.text: Implementation
options.note: Implementation is the deployment of the agreed solution into the business.

options.text: Design
options.note: Design is finished before deployment starts, although it included acceptance testing.

options.text: Realisation
options.note: Realisation comes after deployment and reviews the benefits achieved.

options.text: Definition
options.note: Definition established the requirements much earlier.

options.text: Alignment
options.note: Alignment set the strategic context at the start of the lifecycle.

options.text: Feasibility assessment
options.note: Feasibility assessment belongs to business case work, not to deployment.

questions.explanation: Deployment, training and migration are implementation. Realisation is the tempting near-miss, but it starts once the solution is in operation and is about reviewing benefits.

questions.stem: Six months after go-live, the sponsor asks the analyst to check whether the expected reduction in processing time has actually materialised. Which lifecycle stage is this?

options.text: Realisation
options.note: Realisation covers the post-implementation review and the realisation of business benefits.

options.text: Implementation
options.note: Implementation ended when the solution was deployed and users were supported into live running.

options.text: Design
options.note: Design produced the specification and the tested solution.

options.text: Definition
options.note: Definition established the requirements for the change.

options.text: Alignment
options.note: Alignment confirmed that the change fitted the business strategy.

options.text: The business case
options.note: The business case is the central element that benefits are measured against, not a lifecycle stage.

questions.explanation: Benefits are reviewed in realisation once the solution is in operation. Checking the benefit makes the business case relevant, but the work being done is the realisation review.

questions.stem: In the business change lifecycle, which element sits at the centre and is linked to every stage?

options.text: The business case
options.note: The business case is shown at the centre of the lifecycle and connects to alignment, definition, design, implementation and realisation.

options.text: The design specification
options.note: A design specification is produced during the design stage and is an output of one stage.

options.text: The benefits plan
options.note: Benefits are reviewed in realisation, but the plan is not the hub around which the other stages turn.

options.text: The requirements catalogue
options.note: Requirements are established mainly during definition and then managed through later stages.

options.text: The enterprise architecture
options.note: Enterprise architecture is one of the inputs to alignment.

options.text: The stakeholder map
options.note: Stakeholder analysis supports the work at every stage but is not the central element of the model.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle diagram places the business case in the middle, with a connection to each of the five stages. Every stage is judged against whether the case for the change still stands.

questions.stem: Why does the business change lifecycle treat IT system development as one part of a change rather than the whole of it?

options.text: Because benefits usually depend on changes to processes, roles and skills as well as technology, so the change has to be aligned with business need.
options.note: The lifecycle reflects a broader view of business change, in which technology is only one of the aspects that has to change.

options.text: Because outsourced suppliers cannot be trusted to deliver to specification.
options.note: Outsourcing is one reason organisations value business representation, but it is not the reason the lifecycle is broader than IT development.

options.text: Because enterprise architecture rules out bespoke system development.
options.note: Enterprise architecture is an input to alignment; it does not remove system development from the lifecycle.

options.text: Because Agile methods have replaced linear development lifecycles.
options.note: Agile is one delivery approach among several and does not explain why the lifecycle spans business change.

options.text: Because regulators require benefits to be reported annually.
options.note: External reporting is not the rationale given for the shape of the lifecycle.

options.text: Because the business case is written only after deployment.
options.note: The business case sits at the centre of the lifecycle and is relevant from the start, not only after deployment.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle was developed because organisations recognised that focusing purely on the IT element misses the process, people and organisational changes that actually deliver the benefit.

questions.stem: A warehouse keeps reporting stock discrepancies, and the team asks for a better exception report. The analyst instead traces why stock movements are recorded late at every shift handover. Which principle is being applied?

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: The report request is treated as a symptom, and the analyst investigates the underlying cause of the discrepancies.

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: This principle asks whether the proposed change improves the business at all, but it does not describe tracing a cause.

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: This principle is about evaluating alternative ways of meeting a need, not about diagnosing why a problem occurs.

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements
options.note: This principle filters requests against constraints and objectives, which is a later activity.

options.text: The entire business change lifecycle
options.note: This principle concerns the span of BA involvement, not the depth of investigation.

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: This principle concerns resolving conflicting stakeholder views.

questions.explanation: The request for a report addresses the visible symptom. Checking how and when stock movements are captured looks for the root cause, which is what the first principle asks for.

questions.stem: A sponsor opens a change initiative by saying "we are buying a workflow tool". The analyst asks what business problem the tool is meant to solve and what improvement is expected. Which principle is being applied?

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: The analyst treats IT as an enabler of an agreed business improvement rather than as the purpose of the change.

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: Questioning the tool can look like comparing options, but here the analyst is reframing the goal, not evaluating alternatives.

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: This principle is about diagnosing why a problem occurs, not about questioning the goal of a project.

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements
options.note: This principle filters requirements against constraints once the goal is accepted.

options.text: The entire business change lifecycle
options.note: This principle concerns continuing BA involvement after requirements are defined.

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: This principle concerns handling conflicting stakeholder views.

questions.explanation: The principle says IT systems should enable a business opportunity or the resolution of a business problem. Asking what improvement is expected puts the business outcome ahead of the technology purchase.

questions.stem: The operations director has already selected a vendor product and asks the analyst to write requirements for it. The analyst first sets out and evaluates two other ways of meeting the need, including a process change that needs no software. Which principle is being applied?

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: The analyst challenges a predetermined solution and evaluates alternative options for meeting the business need.

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: This principle is close, but the specific behaviour here is the comparison of alternatives before committing.

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: No investigation into the cause of a problem is described.

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements
options.note: Requirements filtering happens after options are chosen, not instead of choosing between them.

options.text: The entire business change lifecycle
options.note: This principle concerns the span of involvement, not the choice between options.

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: No conflicting stakeholder positions are being resolved.

questions.explanation: The principle asks business analysts to challenge predetermined solutions and identify and evaluate options. The process-only alternative is what makes the challenge concrete.

questions.stem: Stakeholders present 40 requirements they all describe as mandatory. The analyst checks each one against the budget and delivery date, and removes those that add nothing towards the stated business objectives. Which principle is being applied?

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements, not meeting all requests
options.note: The analyst weighs stated requirements against financial and timescale constraints and against business objectives.

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: Stakeholders may be disappointed, but no conflict between stakeholder views is being negotiated here.

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: This principle concerns choosing between ways of meeting the need, not filtering the requirements of one option.

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: The analyst is not investigating why a problem occurs.

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: The analyst is not challenging whether IT is the answer.

options.text: The entire business change lifecycle
options.note: The work described sits within requirements definition.

questions.explanation: The principle accepts that not every request can be met and requires BAs to assess feasibility and contribution to business objectives.

questions.stem: Once the requirements have been signed off, a business analyst hands the pack to the project team and declines to help with design reviews, acceptance testing or the post-implementation review. Which principle is being breached?

options.text: The entire business change lifecycle, not just requirements definition
options.note: The principle expects the BA to support design, testing, deployment and post-implementation review, not only the requirements work.

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: No conflicting stakeholder views are described.

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: The analyst is not being asked to diagnose a problem.

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: The options decision appears to have been taken already.

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements
options.note: No requirements are being filtered in this scenario.

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: The scenario does not turn on the purpose of the technology.

questions.explanation: Requirements definition is one part of the lifecycle. The principle explicitly extends BA responsibility to the whole change, including support for testing, deployment and benefits review.

questions.stem: Sales wants a rule that blocks all discounting without approval; finance wants discounts approved case by case. Both groups have legitimate needs. The analyst brings them together and helps them agree a single rule that satisfies both. Which principle is being applied?

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: The analyst recognises the conflicting views and negotiates a resolution between the stakeholders.

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: A rule is one way of meeting the need, but the behaviour described is the resolution of a conflict.

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: The disagreement is about policy, not about the cause of a problem.

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements
options.note: This principle filters requirements against constraints rather than reconciling two stakeholders.

options.text: The entire business change lifecycle
options.note: This principle concerns when the BA is involved.

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: No technology decision is at issue.

questions.explanation: The principle sets out that business analysts should recognise conflicting stakeholder requirements and negotiate between them rather than record the conflict and move on.

questions.stem: The principles of business analysis are described as being underpinned by two approaches. Which pair?

options.text: The holistic approach and the Agile philosophy
options.note: These are the two approaches named as underpinning the principles.

options.text: The business change lifecycle and the BASF
options.note: These are a lifecycle and a service framework, not the pair that underpins the principles.

options.text: POPIT and the Business Analysis Maturity Model
options.note: POPIT is an analysis model and BAMM is a maturity model; neither is named as an underpinning approach.

options.text: Service thinking and the CMMI
options.note: Service thinking is a perspective on value and CMMI is a process maturity model.

options.text: PESTLE and VMOST
options.note: These are strategy analysis techniques from chapter 3.

options.text: The business case and benefits realisation
options.note: These belong to the lifecycle and to realisation, not to the principles.

questions.explanation: The book states that the principles are underpinned by the holistic approach and the Agile philosophy. The holistic approach supplies the breadth of view, and Agile supplies the flexibility in how requirements and solutions evolve.

questions.stem: A system is delivered on time and works as specified, but the process it supports is unchanged and staff have not been trained, so the expected benefit does not appear. Which of the following does this most clearly show the need for?

options.text: A holistic approach
options.note: The shortfall comes from ignoring parts of the business system beyond the software, which is what a holistic approach prevents.

options.text: Business improvement, not IT system change
options.note: The project did aim at a business improvement; the failure was in the other aspects of the change.

options.text: Root causes, not symptoms
options.note: The problem is not a misdiagnosed cause but an incomplete view of the change.

options.text: Options, not solutions
options.note: Alternative solutions are not at issue here.

options.text: Feasible, contributing requirements
options.note: The requirements were delivered as specified, so filtering is not the issue.

options.text: Negotiation, not avoidance
options.note: No stakeholder conflict is described.

questions.explanation: A holistic approach requires all aspects of the business system, including processes, roles and skills, to be considered together. A software-only view can deliver a working system and still miss the benefit.

questions.stem: A business analyst works with directors to understand which business situations need to improve, defines requirements from a business solution perspective, and models them with conceptual models such as business use case diagrams. Which variant of the role is this?

options.text: Enterprise business analyst
options.note: This variant works on business situations and requirements at a business solution level, often with senior stakeholders and conceptual models.

options.text: Technical business analyst
options.note: This variant analyses solution requirements and models system features, data and events.

options.text: Digital business analyst
options.note: This variant focuses on digital technology, customer experience and data-driven opportunity.

options.text: Project business analyst
options.note: This variant focuses on the software product, typically elaborating user stories.

options.text: Proxy product owner
options.note: This variant owns the product backlog and prioritisation decisions in an Agile team.

options.text: Business systems analyst
options.note: This is an alternative name for the technical or systems analysis variant.

questions.explanation: Senior stakeholder engagement plus business-level requirements and conceptual business use case models is the enterprise variant. The technical variant works at the level of system features and data.

questions.stem: A business analyst models required system behaviour with use case, class and state machine diagrams, and specifies the non-functional requirements that developers must meet. Which variant of the role is this?

options.text: Technical business analyst
options.note: This variant analyses solution requirements and supports software development with system, data and event models.

options.text: Enterprise business analyst
options.note: This variant works at business solution level with senior stakeholders, not at system feature level.

options.text: Digital business analyst
options.note: This variant concentrates on digital opportunity, customer experience and data insight.

options.text: Project business analyst
options.note: This variant elaborates user stories and business rules for the software product rather than modelling system features in detail.

options.text: Proxy product owner
options.note: This variant manages the backlog and feature priorities.

options.text: Strategic analyst
options.note: Strategy analysis and definition is normally senior management work, supported by consultants, and outside the BA remit.

questions.explanation: Detailed system models and non-functional specifications sit with the technical variant, also called the business systems analyst. The essential difference from business analysis is a software focus rather than a business outcome focus.

questions.stem: A business analyst is asked to improve how customers are recognised and served across web and mobile channels, drawing on customer data and analytics, and to challenge existing ways of working using new technology. Which variant of the role is this?

options.text: Digital business analyst
options.note: This variant exploits digital technologies, customer experience requirements and data insight, and extends beyond systems analysis.

options.text: Technical business analyst
options.note: Technology is involved, but this variant specifies system features and models rather than pursuing digital opportunity and customer experience.

options.text: Enterprise business analyst
options.note: This variant works on business situations and requirements with senior stakeholders across the enterprise.

options.text: Project business analyst
options.note: This variant works within a software project on user stories and business rules.

options.text: Proxy product owner
options.note: This variant owns backlog management and prioritisation.

options.text: IT systems analyst
options.note: This role analyses and specifies IT system requirements within a defined scope.

questions.explanation: Customer experience, personalisation, data and analytics, and challenging existing ways of working are the concerns of the digital variant. The digital role extends beyond systems analysis rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: In an Agile team, a business analyst writes user stories with business staff and product developers, and elaborates the business rules and non-functional requirements that apply to the software product. Which variant of the role is this?

options.text: Project business analyst
options.note: This variant focuses on developing the software product, typically elaborating user stories with business staff and developers.

options.text: Technical business analyst
options.note: This variant is close, but it models system features with use case, class and event diagrams rather than elaborating user stories.

options.text: Enterprise business analyst
options.note: This variant works at business solution level with senior stakeholders.

options.text: Digital business analyst
options.note: This variant focuses on digital opportunity and customer experience across channels.

options.text: Proxy product owner
options.note: This variant holds responsibility for the backlog and its priorities.

options.text: Business systems analyst
options.note: This is another name for the technical variant, not the user story role.

questions.explanation: Elaborating user stories and business rules for a software product is the project variant. The technical variant is the near-miss, but its defining work is system and data modelling.

questions.stem: In an Agile software development environment, a business analyst maintains and orders the product backlog and is empowered to decide which features take priority on the organisation's behalf. Which variant of the role is this?

options.text: Proxy product owner
options.note: Where a BA takes on the product owner's backlog and prioritisation duties, the role is described as the proxy product owner.

options.text: Product owner
options.note: The product owner is the business role being represented; the BA acting in it is the proxy.

options.text: Project business analyst
options.note: This variant elaborates user stories but does not hold decision rights over feature priority.

options.text: Enterprise business analyst
options.note: This variant works at business solution level, not on a product backlog.

options.text: Technical business analyst
options.note: This variant specifies system features and non-functional requirements.

options.text: Digital business analyst
options.note: This variant pursues digital opportunity and customer experience.

questions.explanation: The proxy product owner variant exists because the BA represents the business during product development and is empowered to make decisions about feature priority on its behalf.

questions.stem: The POPIT model is used to structure the analysis of a business system. Which four areas does it cover?

options.text: People; organisation; processes; information and technology
options.note: These are the four views shown in the POPIT triangle, with information and technology treated as one band.

options.text: People; processes; technology; strategy
options.note: Strategy is not a POPIT view; it sets the context in which POPIT analysis happens.

options.text: Organisation; culture; processes; data
options.note: Culture and data are aspects considered within POPIT, but they are not two of its four named views.

options.text: People; information; customers; suppliers
options.note: Customers and suppliers are stakeholder categories, not POPIT views.

options.text: Strategy; processes; information; organisation
options.note: Strategy is absent from POPIT and people is missing from this list.

options.text: People; organisation; products; IT systems
options.note: Products are not a POPIT view, and information is missing.

questions.explanation: POPIT stands for People, Organisation, Processes, Information and Technology. The model is used to check that every view of the business system, and the links between them, has been considered.

questions.stem: A review finds that processes are efficient, the software is adequate and staff are skilled and motivated, but nobody is clear who is accountable for what, managers do not encourage cross-functional working, and there is no supportive management style. Which POPIT area is deficient?

options.text: Organisation
options.note: Roles, responsibilities, management style and cross-functional collaboration are the organisational questions in POPIT.

options.text: People
options.note: Skills and motivation are the people questions, and the review says both are satisfactory.

options.text: Processes
options.note: The review says the processes are efficient and well defined.

options.text: Information and technology
options.note: The software is described as adequate and no information problem is reported.

options.text: Business case
options.note: The business case is the central element of the change lifecycle, not a POPIT view.

options.text: Enterprise architecture
options.note: Enterprise architecture is an input to alignment, not one of the four POPIT areas.

questions.explanation: POPIT asks whether roles and responsibilities are well defined, whether management style is supportive and whether cross-functional working is encouraged. All three failures point to organisation, not to the people themselves.

questions.stem: A business analyst is asked to establish whether a proposed self-service portal is viable and to pull together the costs, benefits and risks so that the board can decide whether to fund it. Which BASF service is this?

options.text: Feasibility assessment and business case development
options.note: The service tests viability and assembles the case on which a funding decision is taken.

options.text: Situation investigation and problem analysis
options.note: This service investigates the business situation and defines the problem before options are assessed.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: This service redesigns or improves processes rather than appraising an investment.

options.text: Requirements definition
options.note: This service elicits and specifies what the solution must do, after the decision to proceed.

options.text: Business acceptance testing
options.note: This service confirms that the delivered solution meets business needs.

options.text: Business change deployment
options.note: This service supports the rollout and take-up of the solution.

questions.explanation: Viability plus costs, benefits and risks for a funding decision is feasibility assessment and business case development. Situation investigation is the tempting near-miss, but that work establishes the problem rather than appraising the investment.

questions.stem: Before go-live, a business analyst plans and supports structured tests in which business staff confirm that the solution supports their work and meets the defined business needs. Which BASF service is this?

options.text: Business acceptance testing
options.note: The service confirms, with business staff, that the solution is fit for the business before it is deployed.

options.text: Business change deployment
options.note: Deployment follows acceptance and covers the rollout and take-up of the change.

options.text: Requirements definition
options.note: Requirements were defined earlier and are the baseline the tests are measured against.

options.text: Feasibility assessment and business case development
options.note: This service appraises the investment, not the delivered solution.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: This service changes the process rather than testing a solution against it.

options.text: Situation investigation and problem analysis
options.note: This service establishes the problem at the start of the work.

questions.explanation: Business acceptance testing is the service in which the business confirms the solution meets its needs. Deployment is the tempting near-miss, but it starts after acceptance has been given.

questions.stem: A firm's analysts are expected to hold deep expertise in one area while also working easily with people from other disciplines, so that they solve problems inside their own specialism and still communicate with colleagues elsewhere. Research into the nature of service, including internal service provision, found this mix makes such staff valuable. Which term does the chapter use for this profile?

options.text: Subject matter expertise
options.note: Subject matter expertise is depth in a particular business area, one element of business knowledge.

options.text: Domain knowledge
options.note: Domain knowledge is a general understanding of a business sector, not a combination of depth and breadth.

options.text: The T-shaped professional
options.note: The T-shaped professional holds deep specialist skills plus broad generic skills across other disciplines.

options.text: Specialist discipline
options.note: A specialist discipline is the depth on its own, and the stem also requires breadth.

options.text: Multi-disciplinary breadth
options.note: Multi-disciplinary breadth is only the horizontal bar, not the whole profile.

options.text: Generic skills across other disciplines
options.note: Generic skills are the breadth alone, without the specialist depth the stem also describes.

questions.explanation: The defining feature is the combination of specialist depth and generic breadth. Subject matter expertise and domain knowledge tempt because they are also about depth, but neither includes the breadth across other disciplines.

questions.stem: A business analyst is profiled on the T model in Figure 2.2. Which pairing correctly places two of her competencies on that profile?

options.text: Communication on the breadth side, requirements engineering in the specialist depth
options.note: Personal qualities such as communication give the breadth, while professional techniques such as requirements engineering give the depth.

options.text: Communication in the specialist depth, requirements engineering on the breadth side
options.note: This inverts the two: communication is a personal quality, requirements engineering a professional technique.

options.text: Both on the breadth side, because both are generic skills
options.note: Professional techniques are specific to the business analyst role, so they are not generic breadth.

options.text: Both in the specialist depth, because both are used in analysis
options.note: Communication is a personal quality and sits on the breadth side.

options.text: Communication on the breadth side, commercial awareness in the specialist depth
options.note: Commercial awareness is business knowledge, which also sits on the breadth side.

options.text: Domain knowledge in the specialist depth, data modelling on the breadth side
options.note: This inverts the two: domain knowledge is breadth, data modelling is depth.

questions.explanation: In Figure 2.2 the breadth of the profile is made up of personal qualities and business knowledge, and the specialist stem is made up of professional techniques. Pairing one from each side wrongly places one of them.

questions.stem: A business analyst is trusted across the organisation: finance, operations and IT all welcome her and she adapts her style to each audience. Her process models, though, are thin, and colleagues say they miss how the work really operates. Which development would most directly deepen the specialist part of her profile?

options.text: Data modelling
options.note: Data modelling is a professional technique, but it would not improve the process models her colleagues find thin.

options.text: Influencing
options.note: Influencing is a personal quality and supports the breadth of her profile rather than its depth.

options.text: Commercial awareness
options.note: Commercial awareness is business knowledge, part of the breadth of the profile.

options.text: Facilitation
options.note: Facilitation is a personal quality, part of the breadth of the profile.

options.text: Business process modelling
options.note: Business process modelling is the professional technique that produces the models her colleagues find thin.

options.text: Gap analysis
options.note: Gap analysis is a professional technique, but it compares states rather than describing how work operates.

questions.explanation: The specialist part of the T is made up of the professional techniques, and the weak work is process modelling. Influencing and facilitation are tempting because they are also used in this kind of work, but they are personal qualities and sit on the breadth side.

questions.stem: One analyst has deepened her skills in Agile delivery and works inside a Scrum team; a second has deepened her skills in process improvement and works on business process improvement projects. In the terms of the chapter, how is this difference best described?

options.text: Two different horizontal bars
options.note: The horizontal bar is the generalist breadth and is not what distinguishes the two analysts.

options.text: Variants of the vertical bar
options.note: The chapter says variants of the vertical bar may represent the skills needed by analysts delivering other business analysis services, such as Agile development or process improvement.

options.text: Two levels of the same competency
options.note: The analysts are not described as more or less advanced; what differs is the specialist skill set.

options.text: A move from T-shaped to specialist
options.note: Neither has given up breadth, so neither has left the T shape behind.

options.text: A move from professional techniques to business knowledge
options.note: Both are deepening professional techniques rather than moving into business knowledge.

options.text: A difference in personal qualities
options.note: Personal qualities are breadth, and nothing here suggests they differ.

questions.explanation: The chapter allows the vertical bar to take different forms for analysts working in different service contexts. The tempting reading is that one analyst is simply better than the other, but the difference is the kind of specialist depth, not its level.

questions.stem: An analyst with a strong record in one business area moves onto a cross-departmental change. In design meetings she cannot follow the architects' discussion, and her requirements come back marked unbuildable. How does the T model explain this?

options.text: Her vertical bar is too narrow for her own discipline
options.note: Her own specialist work is not the problem; the failure is in crossing to another discipline.

options.text: She lacks subject matter expertise in the business area
options.note: She has a strong record in that area, so subject matter expertise is not the gap.

options.text: She needs deeper domain knowledge of the sector
options.note: Domain knowledge concerns the sector, not the ability to work with technical colleagues.

options.text: Her horizontal bar is too narrow to work with the technical community
options.note: The horizontal bar carries the generic skills needed to interact with people from another community, here the architects.

options.text: She should move into portfolio management
options.note: Portfolio management is a different competency and does not address the gap.

options.text: Her profile is sound and the project simply needs a technical architect
options.note: The model explains the failure as a gap in the analyst's breadth, not as a mismatch of role.

questions.explanation: The horizontal bar is what lets an analyst communicate with colleagues from other areas. It is tempting to blame the vertical bar whenever work is rejected, but the specialist work is not what failed here.

questions.stem: Figure 2.1 sets out the two bars of the T. Which description matches the labels the chapter gives them?

options.text: Deep knowledge and skill of a specific domain across the top, multi-disciplinary breadth down the stem
options.note: The two labels are the other way round.

options.text: Multi-disciplinary breadth across the top, project management skill down the stem
options.note: Project management is one professional technique, not the label of the stem.

options.text: Commercial awareness across the top, technical skill down the stem
options.note: Commercial awareness is one element of business knowledge, not the label of a bar.

options.text: Breadth of stakeholder contacts across the top, depth of process knowledge down the stem
options.note: The bars describe knowledge and skill rather than contacts, and the stem is not limited to process knowledge.

options.text: Generic consulting skills across the top, specialist IT skills down the stem
options.note: The model is not confined to IT skills, and this is not the labelling used.

options.text: Multi-disciplinary breadth of knowledge and skill across the top, deep knowledge and skill of a specific domain down the stem
options.note: These are the two labels Figure 2.1 gives to the horizontal bar and the vertical bar.

questions.explanation: The horizontal bar is labelled multi-disciplinary breadth of knowledge and skill, and the stem is labelled deep knowledge and skill of a specific domain. Swapping them is the obvious trap, and it is what the first distractor does.

questions.stem: A head of analysis argues for the T-shaped profile when writing a job description for a new analyst. Which justification matches the chapter's reasoning?

options.text: It means the analyst no longer needs specialist skills once breadth is established
options.note: The model requires both: breadth does not replace specialist depth.

options.text: It guarantees the analyst can lead any change programme
options.note: Leadership is a separate personal quality and the model makes no such guarantee.

options.text: It lets analysts solve problems in their specialism and still communicate with colleagues elsewhere
options.note: This is the benefit the chapter attributes to the mix of depth and breadth.

options.text: It applies only to analysts working in Agile teams
options.note: Agile teams are given as one variant of the vertical bar, not as the scope of the model.

options.text: It replaces professional techniques with business knowledge
options.note: Both are needed; the model does not trade one area for another.

options.text: It removes the need for further development once both bars are filled
options.note: The chapter treats skills as developing continuously, not as a qualification to be completed.

questions.explanation: Depth and breadth together are what make such staff valuable: they can work inside their specialism and across other communities. The tempting wrong answers treat the T as a substitute for one bar or the other, or as a guarantee the model does not make.

questions.stem: Figure 2.3 groups every business analysis competency under one of the three areas. Which of these is a professional technique?

options.text: Resilience
options.note: Resilience is a personal quality: the ability to withstand pressure and sustain an argument.

options.text: Political awareness
options.note: Political awareness is a personal quality, about what is acceptable and who holds power.

options.text: Domain knowledge
options.note: Domain knowledge is business knowledge: understanding of the sector the organisation works in.

options.text: Gap analysis
options.note: Gap analysis is a professional technique: comparing a current and a target state.

options.text: Adaptable mindset
options.note: Adaptable mindset is a personal quality, about coping with ambiguity.

options.text: Subject matter expertise
options.note: Subject matter expertise is business knowledge, refined to a particular product line or service.

questions.explanation: Gap analysis is one of the professional techniques, alongside requirements engineering and business process modelling. Every distractor is a real competency from the chapter, but each belongs to one of the other two areas.

questions.stem: A manager hires an analyst with strong facilitation and relationship building but no formal modelling experience, in preference to a strong modeller who works badly with people. Which argument in Table 2.1 supports that choice?

options.text: Techniques are the only competencies that cannot be taught on the job
options.note: The chapter treats techniques as the easier side to acquire.

options.text: Behavioural skills take time to develop and reflect attitude and mindset, so techniques are easier to add
options.note: Table 2.1 makes exactly this point about personal qualities.

options.text: Personal qualities matter less than business knowledge in a change project
options.note: Table 2.1 says behavioural skills are a prerequisite for working with others.

options.text: Behavioural skills are specific to business analysis and cannot be assessed at selection
options.note: They are described as generic rather than specific to the role.

options.text: A modeller without interpersonal skills can be moved into a technical role instead
options.note: The chapter does not offer this as a resolution.

options.text: Personal qualities only matter once the analyst is senior
options.note: The chapter presents them as needed from the start of the role.

questions.explanation: Table 2.1 says it is often easier to give a person with good behavioural skills the techniques they need than to develop behavioural skills in a good technician, because behavioural skills take longer and are bound up with attitude and mindset.

questions.stem: A business analyst writes requirements in the system's own vocabulary and business staff keep rejecting them as incomprehensible. Which personal quality does the chapter treat as the root of this kind of problem?

options.text: Attention to detail
options.note: Attention to detail is about not missing key information, which is not the failure described.

options.text: Relationship building
options.note: Relationship building is about trust and open dialogue, not about the words chosen.

options.text: Team working
options.note: Team working is about collaborating with a range of stakeholders, not about terminology.

options.text: Professionalism
options.note: Professionalism concerns conduct and personal development.

options.text: Communication
options.note: Communication covers adapting language and style to the audience, and the chapter names poor communication as a frequent root cause of business and IT problems.

options.text: Political awareness
options.note: Political awareness concerns what is acceptable and who holds power.

questions.explanation: The chapter calls communication perhaps the most important skill and warns against unfamiliar terms and technical language that confuse business staff. The other qualities are all needed, but none of them is about the language used.

questions.stem: A business analyst is handed a report that contradicts what operational staff have told her. She works through the conflicting figures, asks why each step is done, what value it adds and whether there is another way, and refuses to accept the headline conclusion. Which personal quality is she demonstrating?

options.text: Analytical thinking skills
options.note: Analytical thinking means sifting conflicting data, questioning received wisdom and not accepting things at face value.

options.text: Attention to detail
options.note: Attention to detail is about not missing key information rather than challenging the conclusion.

options.text: Resilience
options.note: Resilience is about withstanding pressure and sustaining an argument under challenge.

options.text: Problem solving
options.note: Problem solving is about understanding the problem before rushing towards a solution.

options.text: Influencing
options.note: Influencing is about bringing others round to a recommended course of action.

options.text: Political awareness
options.note: Political awareness is about reading what is acceptable and who holds power.

questions.explanation: Testing the evidence, questioning the accepted position and refusing a premature conclusion is analytical and critical thinking. Problem solving tempts because it is adjacent, but the activity here is analysis of evidence rather than framing a problem for solution.

questions.stem: A business analyst presents at community events and helps raise standards across the business analysis profession. Using Pullan and Archer's four levels of leadership, which level is this?

options.text: Self
options.note: Self is about a positive mindset and taking responsibility for personal development and the work undertaken.

options.text: Project
options.note: Project is about supporting and influencing others to achieve project goals.

options.text: Organisation
options.note: Organisation is about helping the organisation succeed at an enterprise service level.

options.text: Wider world
options.note: Wider world is working with the business analysis community to enable excellence across the profession.

options.text: Portfolio
options.note: Portfolio is one of the professional techniques, not one of the four leadership levels.

options.text: Enterprise
options.note: Enterprise belongs to enterprise architecture and portfolio work, not to Pullan and Archer's four levels.

questions.explanation: Pullan and Archer set out self, project, organisation and wider world. Work across the professional community is the widest of the four, beyond the analyst's own organisation.

questions.stem: A business analyst must judge whether a proposed service will be viable. She reads the statement of financial position, the income statement and the cash flow forecast, and weighs the commercial pressures on the sector. Which business knowledge competency is she drawing on?

options.text: Domain knowledge
options.note: Domain knowledge is understanding of the sector and its terminology, not of the organisation's finances.

options.text: Business case development
options.note: Business case development is about identifying options and assessing their costs and benefits.

options.text: Commercial awareness
options.note: Commercial awareness covers the sector, the commercial pressures on the organisation and the basics of business finance.

options.text: Organisation structures
options.note: Organisation structures concerns functional, project, matrix, flat and virtual forms.

options.text: Supplier management
options.note: Supplier management concerns procurement and contractual arrangements.

options.text: Subject matter expertise
options.note: Subject matter expertise is detailed knowledge of a particular product line or service, not of the finances.

questions.explanation: The chapter places the sector, commercial pressures and business finance, including the statement of financial position, income statement, ratio analysis and cash flow, under commercial awareness. Business case development tempts because it also involves money, but it is about options and their costs and benefits.

questions.stem: A business analyst joins a team working on one specific insurance product. She already knows the insurance sector well; over two years she learns that product's particular terminology, processes and constraints in enough detail to challenge assumptions made by the business. Which competency has she developed?

options.text: Domain knowledge
options.note: Domain knowledge is the more general understanding of the sector, which she already had.

options.text: Commercial awareness
options.note: Commercial awareness concerns sector pressures and business finance.

options.text: Digital technology
options.note: Digital technology concerns the potential of technology and the approaches technical specialists use.

options.text: Organisation structures
options.note: Organisation structures concerns how divisions and teams are arranged.

options.text: Business case development
options.note: Business case development is about identifying options and assessing their costs and benefits.

options.text: Subject matter expertise
options.note: Subject matter expertise refines domain knowledge to a lower level of detail in a specific product line or service.

questions.explanation: Subject matter expertise is domain knowledge taken down to the level of a particular product line, with its own terminology, processes and constraints. Domain knowledge is the near-miss: right idea, but too general for what she has built up.

questions.stem: A council takes its existing paper planning application and puts the same steps online, so the process runs faster but the way the work is organised is unchanged. Using Ross et al.'s distinction, what is this?

options.text: Digital transformation
options.note: Digital transformation enhances the organisation's value proposition, which this does not do.

options.text: Digitization
options.note: Digitization improves how the organisation operates by applying digital technology to existing activity.

options.text: Robotic process automation
options.note: RPA is one of the technology trends the chapter lists, not the name for this distinction.

options.text: Software as a service
options.note: SaaS is one of the technology trends the chapter lists, not the name for this distinction.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: Process improvement is a professional technique for redesigning processes, not the distinction being drawn.

options.text: Digital technology
options.note: Digital technology is the general heading; the question asks which of Ross et al.'s two terms applies.

questions.explanation: Ross et al. distinguish digitization, which improves how the organisation operates, from digital transformation, which enhances the value proposition. Here the steps are the same and only the medium has changed.

questions.stem: A business analyst is checking that a proposed solution fits the organisation's enterprise architecture. Which set of domains does the chapter identify as the key domains of EA?

options.text: Business, data, applications and infrastructure
options.note: These are the key domains the chapter lists for enterprise architecture.

options.text: Business, process, applications and technology
options.note: Process and technology are not the domains the chapter names.

options.text: Strategy, business, data and applications
options.note: Strategy is the concern of strategy analysis, not a domain in this list.

options.text: Business, information, applications and infrastructure
options.note: Information is close to data but is not the term used for the domain.

options.text: Data, applications, infrastructure and security
options.note: Security is not one of the four domains listed.

options.text: Business, applications, infrastructure and operations
options.note: Operations is not one of the four domains listed.

questions.explanation: The chapter names business, data, applications and infrastructure architecture as the key EA domains, and says analysts need awareness of them so that proposed solutions stay aligned. Each wrong option swaps in a near-synonym or a neighbouring concern.

questions.stem: A business analyst compares the current process model with the proposed one, then compares an off-the-shelf package against the defined requirements. Which professional technique is she applying?

options.text: Business process modelling
options.note: Process modelling produces the models, but comparing the two states is a different technique.

options.text: Requirements engineering
options.note: Requirements engineering defines and manages requirements rather than comparing states.

options.text: Benefits management
options.note: Benefits management plans, monitors and evaluates the benefits set out in a business case.

options.text: Investigation techniques
options.note: Investigation techniques uncover and analyse the root causes of problems.

options.text: Gap analysis
options.note: Gap analysis compares a current and a target state, or a product against defined requirements.

options.text: Data modelling
options.note: Data modelling represents information requirements and business rules.

questions.explanation: Comparing as-is with to-be, or a package with the requirements, is gap analysis. Business process modelling is the tempting answer because it produces the artefacts being compared, but the comparison itself is the technique in use.

questions.stem: A business analyst runs a workshop in which the group uses sticky notes, mind maps and de Bono's Six Thinking Hats to open up options, then arranges the output into a wall display the group can read at a glance. Which professional technique does this describe?

options.text: Facilitation
options.note: Facilitation is the personal quality of running the group well, not the technique used to generate and display ideas.

options.text: Investigation techniques
options.note: Investigation techniques are for uncovering and analysing the current situation.

options.text: Idea generation and visualisation
options.note: The chapter groups dialogue mapping, open space technology, brainstorming, mind mapping, sticky notes and Six Thinking Hats under idea generation and visualisation.

options.text: Requirements engineering
options.note: Requirements engineering is the framework of activities for defining requirements.

options.text: Business modelling
options.note: Business modelling visualises business systems through conceptual models such as the business activity model.

options.text: Stakeholder analysis and management
options.note: Stakeholder analysis identifies stakeholders, assesses their significance and analyses their perspectives.

questions.explanation: The named set of group techniques for stimulating discussion and representing outcomes is idea generation and visualisation. Facilitation is the near-miss: it is the personal quality that makes the session work, but the techniques themselves are a professional technique.

questions.stem: A change programme is already under way when the business analyst finds that a decision taken two years earlier, before the programme began, no longer fits the organisation's stated priorities. She raises it with the sponsor and asks for the decision to be revisited. Which of the benefits of understanding the strategic context is she demonstrating?

options.text: Analysing and discussing strategic approaches and priorities
options.note: This is the ability to hold a conversation about strategy, not to challenge a specific decision already taken.

options.text: Building credibility when discussing the organisation with stakeholders
options.note: Credibility is the standing the analyst earns with stakeholders, not the act of challenging a decision.

options.text: Analysing the effectiveness of the approach, outputs and benefits expected from a change initiative
options.note: This concerns reviewing whether the change is delivering, not revisiting a prior decision.

options.text: Questioning the appropriateness and alignment of decisions taken prior to and during the execution of change
options.note: The analyst is testing an earlier decision against the organisation's strategic priorities, which is exactly the ability described.

options.text: Providing leadership and influence for the delivery of strategically aligned change
options.note: Leadership is about driving the change forward, not about reopening an earlier decision.

options.text: Aligning the change with the enterprise architecture
options.note: Enterprise architecture alignment is part of the alignment stage of the lifecycle, not one of the benefits the chapter lists.

questions.explanation: The chapter lists five abilities that follow from understanding the strategic context, and challenging the fit of decisions made before or during a change is one of them. The near-miss is analysing strategic approaches, which is about discussing strategy rather than testing a decision against it.

questions.stem: An analyst who takes no interest in the organisation's strategy or its wider environment works strictly from the request in front of her. According to the chapter, what risk does this create for the organisation?

options.text: The requirements will be impossible to elicit from stakeholders
options.note: Elicitation depends on access to stakeholders and their knowledge, not on strategic awareness.

options.text: Outputs may be delivered that harm or damage the capabilities of the organisation
options.note: The chapter states that analysts unaware of the strategic context can deliver outputs that harm or cause damage to the organisation's capabilities.

options.text: The change will no longer be aligned with the enterprise architecture
options.note: Alignment with the enterprise architecture is a lifecycle activity; the stated risk is damage to capability.

options.text: Benefits realisation will become impossible to measure
options.note: Benefits are measured against the business case, which does not depend on the analyst reading the strategy.

options.text: The organisation's strategy will have to be rewritten
options.note: Strategy is set by senior management and is not rewritten because one analyst ignores it.

options.text: The business case will be rejected by the sponsor
options.note: The business case is approved by the sponsor before the work proceeds, and the chapter does not link it to this risk.

questions.explanation: The warning is specific: without strategic awareness the analyst can deliver something that works as asked and still damages the capabilities the organisation relies on. That is why the chapter describes strategic awareness as more than background reading.

questions.stem: At the start of a change initiative a business analyst asks three questions: where is the organisation now, where does it want to be, and how will it get there? Which set of building blocks do these questions correspond to?

options.text: Strengths and weaknesses, opportunities and threats, and the SWOT matrix
options.note: These are the outputs of internal and external analysis, not the three building blocks.

options.text: Vision, mission and objectives
options.note: These are elements of VMOST, which is one technique used within internal analysis.

options.text: Political, economic and socio-cultural factors
options.note: These are PESTLE categories, which cover only part of the external analysis.

options.text: People, organisation, processes, information and technology
options.note: These are the POPIT views of a business system, used to structure a target operating model.

options.text: Definition, design and implementation
options.note: These are stages of the business change lifecycle, not building blocks of the strategic context.

options.text: Current state, target state and strategy execution
options.note: These are the three core building blocks, with strategy execution described as the mission or roadmap between the two states.

questions.explanation: The chapter's first figure reduces the strategic context to the current state, the target state and the move between them, labelled strategy execution and described as the mission or roadmap. VMOST and PESTLE feed into that picture rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: A software start-up releases a deliberately minimal product, watches how customers use it, and reshapes the product and its strategy in short cycles as feedback arrives. Which approach to developing strategy does this describe?

options.text: Linear strategy development
options.note: Linear development sets a relatively unchanging strategy, which suits stable conditions rather than short feedback cycles.

options.text: Hybrid strategy development
options.note: Hybrid blends adaptive and linear approaches across different parts of one organisation, which is not what is described here.

options.text: Adaptive strategy development
options.note: Adaptive, also called lean, strategy development is iterative and driven by market and stakeholder feedback.

options.text: PESTLE analysis
options.note: PESTLE is a technique for analysing the external environment, not an approach to developing strategy.

options.text: Performance measurement
options.note: Performance measurement tracks progress towards the target state and is not a strategy development approach.

options.text: Strategic alignment
options.note: Strategic alignment concerns whether strategy fits the organisation's philosophy, not how the strategy is formed.

questions.explanation: The start-up learns by deploying and reacting to feedback, which is the adaptive approach. Adaptive development is associated with non-hierarchical organisations that value feedback, objective decision-making and continuous improvement.

questions.stem: One organisation runs its new product division on short feedback cycles and constant adjustment, while its regulated network division works to a fixed five-year plan that changes only when the regulator moves. How is this organisation's approach to strategy development best described?

options.text: Adaptive
options.note: Adaptive development is iterative throughout, whereas only the product division works that way.

options.text: Linear
options.note: Linear development sets a relatively unchanging strategy, which describes only the network division.

options.text: PESTLE-led
options.note: PESTLE is an external environment technique and does not describe how strategy is formed.

options.text: Resource-led
options.note: A resource audit identifies strengths and weaknesses and does not describe an approach to developing strategy.

options.text: Hybrid
options.note: The organisation blends the adaptive and linear approaches, which the chapter describes as hybrid development.

options.text: Emergent
options.note: The chapter uses the terms adaptive, linear and hybrid, and emergent is not one of them.

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that organisations may blend the two approaches, even between departments of the same organisation, and calls this hybrid strategy development. Both the adaptive and linear labels fit only half of what is described.

questions.stem: A newly elected government makes reform of the energy market one of its stated priorities and instructs departments to act on it, although no legislation has yet been drafted. Which PESTLE factor does this represent?

options.text: Legal
options.note: Legal factors cover law and regulation with legal effect, and the stem says no legislation exists.

options.text: Political
options.note: Decisions and policies of national and local governments are political factors, and no law has been made yet.

options.text: Economic
options.note: Economic factors concern interest rates, inflation, employment, income and exchange rates.

options.text: Socio-cultural
options.note: Socio-cultural factors concern demographics, preferences and habits in society.

options.text: Technological
options.note: Technological factors concern trends in technology and the skills to exploit it.

options.text: Environmental
options.note: Environmental factors concern the natural environment, such as emissions and waste.

questions.explanation: PESTLE separates what governments decide from what the law requires. A stated priority and a direction to departments is a political factor; it becomes a legal factor only when it is enacted.

questions.stem: Interest rates rise sharply, which increases what the organisation pays on its overdraft, and households have less disposable income to spend with it. Which PESTLE factor covers both effects?

options.text: Political
options.note: Political factors concern government policies and decisions, not the cost of borrowing.

options.text: Legal
options.note: Legal factors concern law and regulation, and no rule change is described.

options.text: Socio-cultural
options.note: Socio-cultural factors concern demographics and changes in preferences and habits.

options.text: Economic
options.note: Interest rates, the cost of borrowing and levels of disposable income are all listed as economic factors.

options.text: Technological
options.note: Technological factors concern technology trends and the availability of technology skills.

options.text: Environmental
options.note: Environmental factors concern the natural environment rather than the cost of finance.

questions.explanation: Both the cost of borrowing and consumer spending power sit inside the economic environment, which the chapter describes as covering interest rates, inflation, employment, disposable income, resource costs, growth and exchange rates.

questions.stem: A retailer's customers are ageing, and households are increasingly buying prepared meals instead of cooking from scratch. Which PESTLE factor is this?

options.text: Economic
options.note: Economic factors cover income, prices and growth, not the age profile or eating habits of the population.

options.text: Environmental
options.note: Environmental factors concern emissions, habitats, animal welfare and waste.

options.text: Political
options.note: Political factors concern government and campaign-group policy positions.

options.text: Legal
options.note: Legal factors concern law and regulation affecting the business.

options.text: Technological
options.note: Technological factors concern trends in technology and the skills needed to use it.

options.text: Socio-cultural
options.note: Changes to demographics and changes in preferences and habits are the two socio-cultural examples the chapter gives.

questions.explanation: The chapter places both demographic change and shifts in consumer preference and habit under socio-cultural factors. The demographic element alone would be enough, and the change in buying behaviour confirms it.

questions.stem: Automation tools are now affordable for a small firm, but it cannot recruit people who know how to build and maintain them. Which PESTLE factor covers the recruitment problem?

options.text: Technological
options.note: The chapter lists the availability of new technology and the availability of skills to build and maintain technology platforms as technological factors.

options.text: Economic
options.note: Economic factors cover the cost of resources and the availability of labour, but the shortage here is specifically of technology skills.

options.text: Socio-cultural
options.note: Socio-cultural factors cover demographics and consumer preferences, not the skills needed for a technology platform.

options.text: Legal
options.note: Legal factors cover employment law and other regulation, not the supply of skills.

options.text: Political
options.note: Political factors cover government and campaign-group policy, not labour supply.

options.text: Environmental
options.note: Environmental factors cover the natural environment, not workforce skills.

questions.explanation: PESTLE's technological factor is not limited to the tools themselves; the chapter explicitly includes the availability of skills to build and maintain technology platforms. The economic factor is the near-miss because it covers labour availability, but the skills gap for a technology platform is classed as technological.

questions.stem: New rules on the handling of personal data require the organisation to change how it stores customer records and to appoint a responsible officer. Which PESTLE factor is this?

options.text: Political
options.note: Political factors concern the policies and decisions of governments and campaign groups, not the obligations that follow from enacted rules.

options.text: Economic
options.note: Economic factors concern interest rates, inflation, income and exchange rates.

options.text: Legal
options.note: Data protection law is one of the legal examples the chapter gives, along with employment, competition, health and safety and taxation rules.

options.text: Socio-cultural
options.note: Socio-cultural factors concern demographics and changes in preferences and habits.

options.text: Technological
options.note: Technological factors concern technology trends and the skills to exploit them.

options.text: Environmental
options.note: Environmental factors concern the natural environment, such as emissions and waste.

questions.explanation: Rules that create obligations with legal or regulatory effect are legal factors. The political factor tempts because governments make such rules, but PESTLE classifies the obligation itself as legal once it is in force.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's customers are refusing to buy products with high carbon emissions and heavy packaging, and its investors are asking for a plan to cut waste. Which PESTLE factor is this?

options.text: Political
options.note: Political factors concern the policies and decisions of governments and transnational bodies, not what customers choose to buy.

options.text: Legal
options.note: Legal factors concern law and regulation, and the pressure described is not a legal obligation.

options.text: Socio-cultural
options.note: Socio-cultural factors concern demographics and consumer preferences, not the natural environment.

options.text: Economic
options.note: Economic factors concern costs, prices and growth rather than environmental impact.

options.text: Environmental
options.note: Emissions, waste and animal welfare are the environmental examples given in the chapter.

options.text: Technological
options.note: Technological factors concern technology trends and the skills to use them.

questions.explanation: Carbon emissions, changes to natural habitats, animal welfare and waste disposal and recycling are the chapter's environmental examples. Pressure from customers is the channel through which the factor arrives, but the factor being assessed is environmental.

questions.stem: A charity publishes two statements. The first reads "We provide free legal advice to tenants facing eviction." The second reads "A country where no tenant faces eviction without advice." Which pairing correctly names the two statements, in that order?

options.text: Vision, then mission
options.note: This reverses them: the target state is the second statement, not the first.

options.text: Mission, then vision
options.note: The mission describes what the organisation does, and the vision defines the target state it wants to reach.

options.text: Objective, then mission
options.note: An objective is a specific outcome used to measure progress, not a statement of what the organisation does.

options.text: Strategy, then vision
options.note: A strategy is the long-term approach to reaching the target state, not the description of current activity.

options.text: Mission, then objective
options.note: The second statement describes a desired future state rather than a measurable outcome.

options.text: Tactic, then mission
options.note: A tactic is a detailed means of executing strategy, not an organisation-wide statement of purpose.

questions.explanation: VMOST separates what the organisation does from the state it is trying to reach. The vision is defined without regard to how it will be achieved, and the mission is realised through day-to-day activity.

questions.stem: A tutoring business decides to recruit and retain the best available tutors and to build and share expertise among them. Its managers then set pay rates above the market rate for tutors and introduce a monthly peer-review session. In VMOST terms, what are the pay rates and the peer-review session?

options.text: Strategy
options.note: Strategy is the long-term approach, which in this case is the decision to recruit, retain and develop the best tutors.

options.text: Objectives
options.note: Objectives are the specific outcomes used to guide and measure progress, such as examination results.

options.text: Mission
options.note: The mission is the statement of what the organisation does, not a set of management actions.

options.text: Tactics
options.note: Tactics are the specific and detailed means by which the strategy is executed, adapted as feedback on the strategy arrives.

options.text: Vision
options.note: The vision is the target state the organisation wants to reach.

options.text: Critical success factors
options.note: Critical success factors are the conditions that must be in place to achieve an objective, not the actions taken to create them.

questions.explanation: The chapter's VMOST example separates the strategic decisions, such as recruiting and retaining the best tutors, from the tactics, such as paying above the market rate and running peer review. Tactics are the detailed means and are revised as feedback arrives.

questions.stem: A review finds that the vision and mission are aligned and that the strategy and tactics are consistent with each other. However, the objectives read "improve educational outcomes" and "grow the business", with no measure, no target date and no sense of what would count as success. Which VMOST assessment question does this fail?

options.text: Does a VMOST for the organisation exist?
options.note: A VMOST clearly exists, since vision, mission, strategy and tactics have all been reviewed.

options.text: Are the vision and mission elements aligned?
options.note: The review has already found that they are aligned.

options.text: Does the strategy align to the vision, mission and objectives?
options.note: The review found the strategy consistent, and the weakness described is in the objectives themselves.

options.text: Do the tactics align to the strategy?
options.note: The review found the tactics consistent with the strategy.

options.text: Is the VMOST communicated to and understood by leadership, management and employees?
options.note: Nothing in the stem is about communication or understanding.

options.text: Are the objectives SMART?
options.note: Objectives should be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, and these are none of those things.

questions.explanation: One of the assessment questions asks whether the objectives are SMART. Vague statements with no measure or date cannot be used to guide or measure progress towards the vision and mission, whatever else is aligned.

questions.stem: The board of a housing association has a documented VMOST whose elements are consistent with each other. A staff survey then finds that team leaders and front-line staff cannot say what the vision is or how their work contributes to it. Which VMOST assessment question does this fail?

options.text: Is the VMOST communicated to and understood by leadership, management and employees?
options.note: The chapter asks whether the VMOST is communicated to and understood at all three levels, and the survey shows it is not.

options.text: Does a VMOST for the organisation exist?
options.note: It exists and is documented, so this question is satisfied.

options.text: Are the vision and mission elements aligned?
options.note: Alignment has already been confirmed and is not what the survey tests.

options.text: Are the objectives SMART?
options.note: The survey is about awareness of the vision, not about the quality of the objectives.

options.text: Do the objectives align to and amplify the vision and mission?
options.note: This is an alignment test between elements, not a test of whether staff understand them.

options.text: Does the strategy align to the vision, mission and objectives?
options.note: The elements are already described as consistent with each other.

questions.explanation: VMOST analysis tests both the content of the elements and whether they are known and understood across the organisation. A VMOST that only the board can recite fails the communication test even when every element is well formed.

questions.stem: The aim is to cut the time taken to settle an insurance claim. The change lead identifies three things that must be in place for that to happen: assessors with the right expertise, complete digital evidence at first notification, and clear rules for triaging claims. What are these three things?

options.text: Key performance indicators
options.note: KPIs are quantitative measurements that track achievement, not conditions that must be in place.

options.text: Targets
options.note: Targets are the specific values to be reached, such as a settlement time in working days.

options.text: Critical success factors
