options.note: CSFs are the qualitative descriptions of the factors that must be in place for the organisation to achieve a defined objective.

options.text: Objectives
options.note: The objective is the outcome to be achieved, which here is the reduction in settlement time.

options.text: Business rules
options.note: Triage rules may be business rules, but the other two items are conditions rather than rules, so the set is not a rules category.

options.text: Benefits
options.note: Benefits are the improvements expected from the change, not the conditions that enable them.

questions.explanation: The three items are qualitative conditions that must hold if the objective is to be met, which is the definition of a critical success factor. KPIs and targets come afterwards, as the quantitative measures and values used to track those factors.

questions.stem: For the critical success factor "fast claims settlement", the team reports average settlement time in days, and the board has set five working days as the figure it wants to reach. Which of these is the key performance indicator?

options.text: Five working days
options.note: This is the target, which is the specific value set against the measure rather than the measure itself.

options.text: Fast claims settlement
options.note: This is the critical success factor, the qualitative condition the measure is tracking.

options.text: The objective of faster settlement
options.note: The objective is the outcome being pursued, which the measures and targets support.

options.text: A red, amber or green status
options.note: The RAG status reports the current position against a target; it is not the measure itself.

options.text: Average settlement time in days
options.note: The KPI is the quantitative measure used to track the critical success factor.

options.text: The claims benefits profile
options.note: A benefits profile records an expected benefit and how it will be realised, not current performance.

questions.explanation: The chapter separates the qualitative CSF from the quantitative KPI and from the target. The KPI is the measure, and the target is the value set for it; the RAG status then reports whether the target is being met.

questions.stem: A tutoring business uses the star rating given by each pupil after a session to track both the quality of its tuition and the engagement of its students. What does this illustrate about performance measurement?

options.text: Each critical success factor requires its own separate KPI
options.note: The example shows the opposite, since one measure serves two factors.

options.text: A single KPI can be used to measure more than one critical success factor
options.note: The chapter notes that multiple KPIs can measure one CSF and that a KPI can measure several CSFs, and this is an example of the second.

options.text: A KPI must be qualitative to track a critical success factor
options.note: KPIs are quantitative by definition; it is the CSFs that are qualitative.

options.text: Targets must be agreed before critical success factors are defined
options.note: Targets are set against KPIs, which follow from the CSFs.

options.text: Critical success factors are derived from the KPIs they measure
options.note: The direction is the other way: KPIs are chosen to track CSFs.

options.text: A KPI can only be reported once a target has been met
options.note: Reporting against a target happens continuously through the RAG status.

questions.explanation: Sharing a measure across two factors keeps reporting consistent and aligned with the objective. The chapter makes the point explicitly in its private tuition example, where the session star rating is used for both the quality of tuition and student engagement.

questions.stem: An organisation's critical success factors all concern cost reduction and profit margin, and its performance reporting covers nothing else. The chapter warns that this emphasis is too narrow. Which framework does it name as the means of balancing performance measures?

options.text: PESTLE
options.note: PESTLE assesses the external environment and does not balance internal performance measures.

options.text: VMOST
options.note: VMOST analyses the internal strategic environment but does not provide a set of performance perspectives.

options.text: SWOT
options.note: SWOT summarises internal and external analysis rather than balancing measures.

options.text: The balanced scorecard
options.note: The BSC assesses the breadth and balance of goals across financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth measures.

options.text: POPIT
options.note: POPIT structures the views of a business system and does not define performance perspectives.

options.text: The growth share matrix
options.note: The growth share matrix analyses the product portfolio, not the balance of performance measures.

questions.explanation: The chapter says CSFs are ideally balanced using the BSC and that an over-reliance on financial measures has limited attention to process, learning and growth, and customer performance. The BSC is the framework that supplies those four perspectives.

questions.stem: A business analyst is populating a SWOT matrix. Which of these entries belongs in the threats quadrant?

options.text: Demographic change that opens a larger market for the organisation's products
options.note: This is external but favourable, so it belongs with opportunities.

options.text: A high level of customer satisfaction against target
options.note: This is internal and favourable, so it is a strength.

options.text: A gap in leadership succession plans
options.note: This is internal and unfavourable, so it is a weakness.

options.text: New technology that lowers the cost of delivering the service
options.note: This is external and favourable, so it is an opportunity.

options.text: A strong record of exceeding customer-focused objectives
options.note: This is internal and favourable, so it is a strength.

options.text: New data protection rules that raise the cost of holding customer records
options.note: A change in the legal environment that works against the organisation is an external threat.

questions.explanation: SWOT has two axes. Internal and external decides where an entry sits, and favourable or unfavourable decides which quadrant. The regulatory change is both external and unfavourable, which makes it a threat.

questions.stem: A team is deciding what to put in the strengths and weaknesses quadrants of a SWOT. Which set of techniques does the chapter say should supply these entries?

options.text: VMOST analysis, performance measurement, the resource audit and the growth share matrix
options.note: These are the internal environment techniques, and they are the sources of strengths and weaknesses.

options.text: PESTLE analysis and Porter's Five Forces
options.note: These analyse the external environment, so they supply opportunities and threats instead.

options.text: POPIT and the business model canvas
options.note: These are strategy execution techniques, not sources of strengths and weaknesses.

options.text: PESTLE analysis and VMOST analysis
options.note: Only the VMOST half is internal, so this set mixes the two environments.

options.text: The growth share matrix and Porter's Five Forces
options.note: The growth share matrix is internal, but Five Forces analyses the industry environment.

options.text: Scenario analysis and prototyping
options.note: These are investigation and requirements techniques, not internal environment analysis.

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that strengths and weaknesses are found inside the organisation, through VMOST, performance measurement, the resource audit and analysis of the product portfolio. PESTLE and Five Forces are the near-miss because they are also named in the chapter, but they belong to the external half.

questions.stem: A SWOT is produced in a two-hour workshop from managers' opinions alone, with no VMOST, resource audit, performance measurement, PESTLE or Five Forces work behind it. What is the chapter's objection to this?

options.text: A SWOT should contain an equal number of entries in each quadrant
options.note: The chapter sets no such rule, and balance between quadrants is not the objection.

options.text: A SWOT should express every entry as a KPI with a target
options.note: Entries are descriptive; the chapter asks for accuracy, completeness, brevity and clarity, not quantification.

options.text: The SWOT should be built from the internal and external analysis, or strategic decisions will rest on insufficiently robust information
options.note: The chapter requires the SWOT to be developed using the techniques described for each environment, precisely so that it reflects the organisation's position accurately.

options.text: A SWOT should be kept short, so each entry must fit on one line
options.note: Brevity is required, but the objection here is the missing analysis rather than the length of the entries.

options.text: A SWOT replaces the need for PESTLE and Five Forces analysis
options.note: The SWOT summarises those analyses and does not substitute for them.

options.text: A SWOT should describe the target state rather than the current position
options.note: The SWOT summarises the current strategic position, not the target state.

questions.explanation: The chapter warns that a SWOT assembled without the underlying analysis can lead to ill-considered strategic decisions based on insufficiently robust information. Its content and language also have to be accurate, complete, brief and clear, and aligned with the VMOST.

questions.stem: A completed SWOT lists an ageing customer base as a threat and a new regional trade agreement as an opportunity. According to the chapter, what is within the organisation's control?

options.text: The demographic trend behind the threat
options.note: Demographic change comes from outside the organisation and cannot be influenced by it.

options.text: The terms of the trade agreement
options.note: The agreement is made by governments and is outside the organisation's control.

options.text: The actions of its competitors
options.note: Competitor behaviour is part of the external environment.

options.text: The political climate in the region
options.note: Political factors are part of the macro environment beyond the organisation's immediate control.

options.text: Whether it acts to grasp the opportunity or to deal with the threat
options.note: The external factors cannot be influenced, but the decisions about how to respond to them are within the organisation's control.

options.text: The pace of technological change in its market
options.note: Technology trends are external factors, not something the organisation controls.

questions.explanation: The chapter's key point about SWOT is that opportunities and threats are found outside the organisation and cannot be influenced by it, whereas the decisions about whether to grasp an opportunity or deal with a threat are within its control. The SWOT is the input to those decisions, not a means of changing the external factors.

questions.stem: A business analyst sets out nine areas covering key partners, key activities, key resources, value propositions, customer relationships, channels, customer segments, cost structure and revenue streams, so that the organisation can describe how it creates, delivers and captures value. Which strategy execution technique is this?

options.text: The target operating model
options.note: A TOM describes how the business needs to be set up to execute strategy, not how value is created and captured.

options.text: The business model canvas
options.note: The BMC is the generic template of nine elements that describes how an organisation creates, manages and delivers value.

options.text: The business capability model
options.note: A BCM is a pictorial view of what the organisation can do, not a description of value creation and revenue.

options.text: Value stream modelling
options.note: A value stream model shows the activities that produce a value item for a stakeholder, not the whole business model.

options.text: VMOST
options.note: VMOST analyses the internal strategic environment and has five elements, not nine.

options.text: POPIT
options.note: POPIT structures the views of a business system and does not cover customers, revenue and cost.

questions.explanation: The nine areas listed are the elements of the business model canvas set out in the chapter's table. The target operating model is the nearest alternative, but it answers how the business is set up to execute strategy rather than how value is created and captured.

questions.stem: On the business model canvas, one area asks which customer problems the organisation's products or services solve, which opportunities they support, and what makes them worth choosing over the alternatives. Which element of the canvas is this?

options.text: Customer segments
options.note: Customer segments asks who the important customers are and for whom the value is proposed.

options.text: Channels
options.note: Channels asks how the organisation interacts with and reaches its customers.

options.text: Customer relationships
options.note: Customer relationships asks what relationship exists with each segment and how it might be improved.

options.text: Value proposition
options.note: The value proposition element asks what value is offered, which problems it solves and what qualities make the offer attractive.

options.text: Key activities
options.note: Key activities asks what activities the value proposition, channels and relationships require.

options.text: Revenue streams
options.note: Revenue streams asks where income comes from and how profitable each stream is.

questions.explanation: The value proposition is the canvas element that describes the offer itself. Customer segments is the tempting near-miss because it also mentions the customer, but it asks who they are rather than what is being offered to them.

questions.stem: A strategy has been agreed and the analyst must now describe how the business needs to be set up to deliver it, at a more detailed level than a business model canvas allows: the knowledge and skills required, the structure and culture, the processes, the information, and the technology. The result will be compared with the current state to identify what has to change. Which approach fits?

options.text: A business model canvas
options.note: The canvas describes how value is created and captured, not how the business is set up to deliver an agreed strategy.

options.text: A value stream model
options.note: A value stream model shows the activities that produce a value item for a stakeholder, not the whole operating model.

options.text: A business capability model
options.note: A BCM shows what the organisation can do, not how people, processes, information and technology will be arranged.

options.text: A VMOST analysis
options.note: VMOST analyses the internal strategic environment and does not describe a future operating state.

options.text: A PESTLE analysis
options.note: PESTLE analyses the external environment and says nothing about how the business will operate.

options.text: A target operating model structured using POPIT
options.note: A TOM describes how the business needs to be established to support the execution of strategy, and POPIT is the view that covers all five areas listed.

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the TOM as the means of describing how the business needs to be established to support strategy execution, more detailed than the canvas or value stream, and names POPIT as the view that covers people, organisation, processes, information and technology. That also makes the TOM a basis for gap analysis against the current state.

questions.stem: A central team of business analysts takes work as it comes and cannot say what it offers or what difference it makes. Its head wants a published description of each service the team provides, with the value it offers and the activities and techniques used to deliver it. Which framework supplies this?

options.text: The business change lifecycle
options.note: The lifecycle sequences the stages of one change initiative and says nothing about a portfolio of services.

options.text: The Business Analysis Maturity Model
options.note: BAMM grades the maturity of BA practice, not the services on offer and their value.

options.text: The Business Analysis Service Framework
options.note: The BASF defines a portfolio of services, each with a value proposition, the activities needed to perform it and the techniques applied.

options.text: The POPIT model
options.note: POPIT is a way of viewing the parts of a business system, not a service catalogue.

options.text: The business analyst role variants
options.note: Role variants describe how the role is specialised in different organisations, not what the service offers.

options.text: The OSCAR terms of reference
options.note: OSCAR clarifies the terms of a single assignment, not the portfolio of services a team provides.

questions.explanation: The BASF was created to clarify the BA role and the benefit it brings by defining a portfolio of services, each with a value proposition, activities and techniques. BAMM is the tempting confusion because it also describes the BA role, but it grades maturity rather than defining services.

questions.stem: Before starting an assignment, a business analyst confirms the terms of reference. The organisation insists on a specified modelling notation, a prescribed documentation template and a fixed set of review gates. Which OSCAR element covers these?

options.text: Scope
options.note: Scope defines the area of business to be investigated and the deliverables, not the standards the work must follow.

options.text: Objectives
options.note: Objectives state the business and project outcomes to be achieved.

options.text: Authority
options.note: Authority identifies who approves the objectives and signs off the deliverables.

options.text: Constraints
options.note: Constraints cover time, budgetary and policy limits and the organisational standards on methods, approaches, techniques and tools.

options.text: Resources
options.note: Resources are the human, financial and physical means available for the work.

options.text: Value proposition
options.note: A value proposition states the benefit a service offers to its customers.

questions.explanation: Table 4.1 lists constraints as the time, budgetary and policy limits plus the organisational standards on methods, techniques and tools. A mandated notation and template set is exactly such a standard, which is why scope is the wrong answer even though it also appears in the terms of reference.

questions.stem: A business analyst is planning communication for a service. The sponsor, the executives and the business owners sit in one ring of the recipients model, one ring outside the users and support staff. Which ring is theirs?

options.text: Project stakeholders
options.note: The project ring holds domain experts, product owners, testers and developers, closest to the solution.

options.text: Governance stakeholders
options.note: The governance ring sits outside the operational ring and holds business owners, executives and the sponsor.

options.text: Operational stakeholders
options.note: The operational ring holds the business users and support staff who run the process day to day.

options.text: External stakeholders
options.note: The external ring holds governments, suppliers, partners, regulators and customers.

options.text: Service beneficiaries
options.note: Beneficiaries are those who gain from the change, and the model groups recipients by their relationship to the work rather than by benefit.

options.text: Domain experts
options.note: Domain experts sit in the project ring, not with the executives and the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Figure 4.8 nests four rings: project, operational, governance and external. Executives, business owners and the sponsor are governance stakeholders, whose interest is oversight and approval rather than day-to-day operation.

questions.stem: A senior business analyst is asked to work with the board on which business system should be put in place to deliver a new corporate strategy, before any project has been defined. Which service, beyond the core services, does this describe?

options.text: IT requirements specification
options.note: This service applies modelling techniques such as UML to specify functional and non-functional requirements.

options.text: Situation investigation and problem analysis
options.note: This core service investigates root causes and shapes a project, but it starts from an existing problem rather than from corporate strategy.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: This core service redesigns processes for efficiency and effectiveness rather than choosing a business system for a strategy.

options.text: Feasibility assessment and business case development
options.note: This core service appraises options once a change is in view; it does not define the business system that will deliver a strategy.

options.text: Strategy analysis and execution
options.note: This service has analysts working closely with senior management to define the most effective business system to implement elements of the business strategy.

options.text: Enterprise architecture
options.note: Enterprise architecture is an input to the strategic context, not a service delivered by a business analyst.

questions.explanation: The book names two services beyond the core: strategy analysis and execution, and IT requirements specification. Working with senior management on the business system that will implement strategy is the first of them, which is why situation investigation is the near-miss rather than the answer.

questions.stem: In one organisation the business analyst models system features with use case diagrams, data with class diagrams and system behaviour with state machine diagrams, then writes the functional and non-functional requirements for the developers. Which service is this?

options.text: Requirements definition
options.note: This core service elicits and defines requirements for business and IT change, but the system modelling and specification described here goes further.

options.text: Strategy analysis and execution
options.note: This service works with senior management on the business system that will implement a strategy.

options.text: Business acceptance testing
options.note: This service supports business staff in testing a delivered solution against their needs.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: This service redesigns and implements business processes rather than specifying a system.

options.text: The technical business analyst role
options.note: This is a role variant focused on solution requirements, and the question asks which service is being delivered.

options.text: IT requirements specification
options.note: This service uses modelling techniques such as those from UML to specify functional and non-functional requirements.

questions.explanation: System feature, data and event modelling plus functional and non-functional specification is IT requirements specification, one of the two services beyond the core. Requirements definition is the near-miss because it also produces requirements, but it works at business level rather than specifying the system in modelling detail.

questions.stem: Customer complaints have risen and management blames the call-centre system. The analyst sets a target view of the business system built from a business activity model, compares the current situation with it, and identifies where action is needed. What is this comparison called?

options.text: Root cause analysis
options.note: Root cause analysis looks for the underlying cause of a problem rather than comparing two views of the business system.

options.text: Problem definition
options.note: Defining the problem states what is to be addressed; it does not compare the current and target views.

options.text: Business process modelling
options.note: Process modelling describes how work is carried out, at a more detailed level than this conceptual target view.

options.text: Gap analysis
options.note: Gap analysis compares an 'as is' view with a desired 'to be' view in order to identify where action is needed.

options.text: Options analysis
options.note: Options analysis evaluates alternative ways of meeting the need and comes later in the service.

options.text: Benefits realisation
options.note: Benefits realisation is the later review of whether the expected benefits appeared.

questions.explanation: The situation investigation service uses gap analysis, comparing an 'as is' view with a 'to be' view, and a business activity model can supply that conceptual target. Root cause analysis is tempting because complaints are a symptom, but the question asks what the comparison itself is called.

questions.stem: A business analyst finishes investigating a business situation and concludes that the proposed change should not go ahead. The sponsor asks for the reasoning to be recorded formally. Which activity of the situation investigation and problem analysis service is this?

options.text: Define the problem
options.note: The problem has already been defined; this activity records why no project should follow.

options.text: Define the rationale for rejecting a project proposal
options.note: The activities of the service include defining the rationale for rejecting a proposal as well as defining the scope of a project that does proceed.

options.text: Define the scope of the business change project
options.note: Scoping applies where the project is going ahead, and here the conclusion is that it should not.

options.text: Support comparison and selection of solution
options.note: Comparing options belongs to feasibility assessment and business case development.

options.text: Assess business readiness
options.note: Business readiness is assessed in business change deployment.

options.text: Negotiate stakeholder conflicts
options.note: Negotiating conflicts between stakeholders belongs to stakeholder engagement.

questions.explanation: Defining the rationale for rejecting a project proposal is listed as one of the six activities of this service, alongside defining the scope of a project that does proceed. Scoping is the near-miss, but it presupposes an approved project.

questions.stem: A business case has been approved in principle. The finance director now wants the chosen IT system specified in full detail before the project starts, so that the case can be finalised. How does the feasibility assessment and business case development service treat this?

options.text: Costs and benefits are quantified only after the solution has been built
options.note: Costs and benefits are quantified in this service, before the funding decision is taken.

options.text: Technical feasibility is assessed during business acceptance testing
options.note: Technical feasibility is evaluated while the options are assessed, long before testing.

options.text: Options are defined in outline here, with detailed IT options evaluated later and the case revisited
options.note: The service works at outline level sufficient for a decision, and detailed options for the IT system come later.

options.text: The case is developed only after the solution has been designed in detail
options.note: The case supports the decision to invest, so it precedes detailed design.

options.text: Option generation is deferred until the requirements are defined
options.note: Options are generated and evaluated within this service, before requirements definition.

options.text: A business case cannot be revisited once it has been approved
options.note: The book states that the case may be revisited when the detailed IT options are evaluated.

questions.explanation: The changes considered at this stage are defined in outline only, in enough detail to support a decision; where IT systems are needed the detailed options are evaluated later and the case revisited. Treating approval as final gets this backwards.

questions.stem: An analyst has a long list of ways to close a service gap. Two cannot be delivered at all: one needs a capability the organisation will never have, and one would breach a statutory duty. The analyst sets both aside before costing anything. Which activity of the feasibility assessment and business case development service is this?

options.text: Generate and describe options to resolve the problem
options.note: Generating options produced the list, and screening it is a separate activity.

options.text: Identify and analyse costs and benefits for each option
options.note: Costing applies to the options that survive the screening.

options.text: Identify and analyse impacts and risks for each option
options.note: Impact and risk analysis applies to the options that remain.

options.text: Evaluate financial, technical and business feasibility of the options
options.note: Feasibility is evaluated for the options left after unviable ones are removed.

options.text: Remove unviable options
options.note: The service screens out options that cannot be delivered before the rest are analysed in detail.

options.text: Evaluate alignment of options with strategic goals
options.note: Strategic alignment is judged for the options that remain.

questions.explanation: Removing unviable options is the second activity of the service and is a screening step taken before costs, benefits, impacts and risks are analysed for what remains. Feasibility evaluation is the near-miss, but that is the fuller assessment of options that have already passed the screen.

questions.stem: A retailer's order-to-cash process takes twelve days and crosses sales, the warehouse and finance. The analyst models how it works now, defines a revised process with those three areas, and identifies the actions needed to put it in place. Which service is this?

options.text: Situation investigation and problem analysis
options.note: This service investigates and defines the problem rather than redesigning a process that is already in view.

options.text: Requirements definition
options.note: This service defines what a solution must do; here the process itself is being redesigned.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: This service models existing processes, defines required processes and identifies the actions needed to implement them.

options.text: Feasibility assessment and business case development
options.note: This service appraises options and builds the case for investment.

options.text: Business change deployment
options.note: This service supports the transition and adoption once the new process is agreed.

options.text: Business acceptance testing
options.note: This service supports business staff in testing a change before it goes live.

questions.explanation: Modelling the current process, defining the revised one and identifying implementation actions is business process improvement. Situation investigation is the near-miss, but the problem has already been framed here and the work is the redesign itself.

questions.stem: After redesigning the purchase-to-pay process, the analyst checks that the new approval steps, the routing rules in the workflow tool and the postings in the finance system all match the redesigned process. Which activity of business process improvement is this?

options.text: Model existing processes
options.note: Modelling records how the process works now, which happened before the redesign.

options.text: Identify gaps between existing and required processes
options.note: This identifies what has to change, not whether systems match the new design.

options.text: Analyse the gaps between existing and required processes
options.note: Analysing gaps explains their causes and implications.

options.text: Identify and analyse business process measures
options.note: Process measures assess performance rather than consistency between systems and process.

options.text: Ensure alignment between IT systems and processes
options.note: This activity checks that systems support the redesigned process rather than working against it.

options.text: Identify actions to implement new processes
options.note: This identifies implementation steps; it does not check that systems match the design.

questions.explanation: Ensuring alignment between IT systems and processes is one of the seven activities of the service, and it matters because a redesigned process fails if the supporting systems still enforce the old steps. Identifying implementation actions is the near-miss, but the work described is checking consistency, not planning the rollout.

questions.stem: A business analyst is defining what a department needs in order to comply with a new regulation. The work concludes that no system change is needed: the need can be met by rewriting two job descriptions and running a training course. Which service is being delivered?

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: No process is being redesigned; the work is deciding what the department must have in place.

options.text: Requirements definition
options.note: This service defines requirements for business and IT change, including needs that are met without new technology.

options.text: Business change deployment
options.note: Deployment covers training delivery and adoption once the change is agreed, not the definition of the need.

options.text: Business acceptance testing
options.note: Testing confirms that a delivered solution meets the need.

options.text: Situation investigation and problem analysis
options.note: This investigates and defines the problem rather than specifying what is required.

options.text: Feasibility assessment and business case development
options.note: This appraises options and assembles the case for investment.

questions.explanation: Requirements definition covers requirements for business change as well as IT change, and the book gives rewritten job descriptions and additional training as examples of needs met without a new system. Deployment is the tempting error because training appears in both services, but here the training has not been designed or delivered yet.

questions.stem: At the start of requirements work on a large programme, the analyst agrees how requirements will be elicited, recorded and reviewed, and sets the quality standards each requirement must meet. Which activity of requirements definition is this?

options.text: Elicit and interpret the requirements
options.note: Elicitation gathers the requirements themselves, which happens after the approach is agreed.

options.text: Analyse, prioritise and assure the quality of the defined requirements
options.note: This checks defined requirements against the standards; it does not set them.

options.text: Establish traceability from the business need to the solution
options.note: Traceability links requirements to their origins and onwards to the solution.

options.text: Support stakeholder review of the requirements
options.note: Review confirms the requirements with stakeholders once they have been recorded.

options.text: Agree the scope of the testing activity
options.note: Agreeing test scope belongs to business acceptance testing.

options.text: Define the requirements definition approach and quality standards
options.note: The first activity of the service sets the approach and the standards the requirements must meet.

questions.explanation: Defining the approach and the quality standards is the first activity of requirements definition, and it is what makes the rest of the work consistent across a large programme. Assuring quality is the near-miss, but that is checking requirements against standards rather than setting them.

questions.stem: Two weeks before go-live, business managers say they have no time to test and ask the analyst to approve the solution on their behalf. What is the correct position under the business acceptance testing service?

options.text: The analyst should sign it off because they wrote the requirements
options.note: Writing the requirements does not transfer responsibility for acceptance to the analyst.

options.text: The sponsor should sign it off because they approved the business case
options.note: Approving the case is a funding decision, not acceptance of the solution.

options.text: The supplier's test evidence should be accepted instead of business testing
options.note: Supplier testing does not establish that the solution fits the business need.

options.text: Responsibility stays with business staff, and the analyst helps them find the time and design the tests
options.note: The service expects business staff to own acceptance, with the analyst supporting them in it.

options.text: Acceptance should be deferred to the post-implementation review
options.note: The review happens after deployment, when the solution is already in use.

options.text: The project manager should accept on the business's behalf
options.note: The project manager delivers the solution and cannot substitute for business acceptance.

questions.explanation: Responsibility for business acceptance testing rests with business staff, and the analyst's role is to help them discharge it by making sure managers understand why it matters, encouraging them to allocate time, and assisting with test design and recording. Signing off on their behalf removes the only check that the solution fits the business.

questions.stem: Before go-live the analyst works through a seven-element checklist covering customers, processes, the organisation, location, data, applications and technology, to judge whether the business can take the change. Which technique is this?

options.text: CPPOLDAT
options.note: CPPOLDAT provides this seven-element checklist for assessing business readiness.

options.text: POPIT
options.note: POPIT covers people, organisation, processes, information and technology, and has no customer, location or application views.

options.text: CATWOE
options.note: CATWOE is used to structure a root definition around customers, actors, transformation and world view.

options.text: OSCAR
options.note: OSCAR sets out the terms of reference for a service: objectives, scope, constraints, authority and resources.

options.text: RACI
options.note: RACI allocates responsibility for activities and decisions.

options.text: VMOST
options.note: VMOST expresses vision, mission, objectives, strategy and tactics.

questions.explanation: Business readiness can be assessed with POPIT or CPPOLDAT, and only CPPOLDAT has the seven elements of customer, process, organisation, location, data, applications and technology. POPIT is the near-miss because it is also used for readiness, but its views do not match the list.

questions.stem: Three months after go-live the analyst is still involved, helping the business measure whether the expected efficiency gain has appeared and supporting the post-implementation review. Which BASF service does this work belong to?

options.text: Business acceptance testing
options.note: Acceptance testing happens before deployment, not months after it.

options.text: Business process improvement
options.note: This service redesigns and implements processes rather than reviewing the benefits they delivered.

options.text: Business change deployment
options.note: The service includes supporting benefits and post-implementation reviews and supporting the realisation of business benefits.

options.text: Feasibility assessment and business case development
options.note: This service predicts and appraises benefits before the investment decision is taken.

options.text: Situation investigation and problem analysis
options.note: This service investigates the original situation at the start of the work.

options.text: Realisation
options.note: Realisation is a stage of the business change lifecycle, not one of the BASF services.

questions.explanation: Business change deployment runs past go-live: its activities include supporting the benefits and post-implementation reviews and supporting the realisation of business benefits. Realisation is the tempting answer because it names the same work, but it is a lifecycle stage rather than a service in the framework.

questions.stem: A business analyst has one week and a small budget to reconcile the conflicting views of three departments on how a claims process should work, and the managers must leave with an agreed way forward. Which technique fits?

options.text: A focus group
options.note: A focus group gathers opinions from a sample and deliberately does not seek consensus or give the group ownership.

options.text: A series of one-to-one interviews
options.note: Interviews would take longer and would not bring the three departments to an agreed position.

options.text: Observation
options.note: Observation shows how work is done now rather than reconciling views about a future process.

options.text: A workshop
options.note: A workshop brings stakeholders together to explore viewpoints and reach consensus within tight time and budget.

options.text: A survey
options.note: A survey collects a limited amount of information from many people and cannot reconcile conflicting views.

options.text: Document analysis
options.note: Document analysis reviews existing records and cannot produce agreement between departments.

questions.explanation: Consensus, speed and buy-in are workshop advantages, and the chapter says workshops are especially valuable when time and budgets are tight and several viewpoints must be reconciled. A focus group is the near miss because it also gathers a group, but it aims to elicit opinions rather than to reach agreement.

questions.stem: A workshop agrees a new approvals route, but a week later the decisions are reversed by managers who were not in the room. The organisation has a strong hierarchy in which power radiates from a few central people. Which workshop disadvantage does this illustrate?

options.text: Extensive preparation time
options.note: Preparation delay shows as difficulty arranging the session, not as decisions being overturned afterwards.

options.text: Authority limitations
options.note: Participants lacked the authority to commit, which the chapter says is worse where power radiates from a few people or the hierarchy is strong.

options.text: Undue influence of dominant personalities
options.note: A dominant personality would skew the discussion in the room rather than cause a later reversal.

options.text: Absence of buy-in and acceptance
options.note: Lack of buy-in shows as resistance to the outcome, not as managers reversing a decision.

options.text: A consensus view that was too broad
options.note: A broad consensus would be harder to reverse, not easier.

options.text: A limited view of the area under investigation
options.note: A narrow view leaves issues uncovered rather than reversing decisions already made.

questions.explanation: The disadvantage is authority limitations: the wrong people, or people without the power to commit, attend and the decisions do not stick. Dominant personalities is the tempting confusion because it is also about who controls the room, but its effect is a skewed discussion, not a reversal by absent managers.

questions.stem: A facilitator has a group of knowledgeable but reticent participants. She wants each of them to write ideas down and to develop ideas that colleagues have already started. Which discovery technique should she use?

options.text: Brainstorming
options.note: Brainstorming asks people to call ideas out, which this group will not do.

options.text: A round robin
options.note: A round robin gives each person a spoken turn but does not let them build on written ideas.

options.text: A Post-it note exercise
options.note: Sticky notes are written individually and grouped afterwards, so ideas are not developed by others first.

options.text: Stepwise refinement
options.note: Stepwise refinement drills into one statement by repeated questioning rather than generating ideas.

options.text: Break-out groups
options.note: Break-out groups divide a large workshop into small teams and do not address reluctance to contribute.

options.text: Brainwriting
options.note: Sheets carrying an idea circulate and each participant adds to them in writing, which suits people unwilling to speak up.

questions.explanation: Brainwriting exists to overcome the problem of participants who will not interrupt or call out, while still letting them build on the ideas of others. The Post-it note exercise is the near miss because it is also silent and written, but ideas are generated individually and grouped afterwards rather than developed in sequence.

questions.stem: A workshop group needs a diagram showing the tasks in a process, the actors responsible for each and the order in which they happen, so that they can agree how the work is done today. Which visualisation technique should the facilitator use?

options.text: A rich picture
options.note: A rich picture is deliberately unstructured and shows human and cultural aspects rather than a task sequence.

options.text: A business process model
options.note: A process model shows the tasks, the actors and the flow of the process.

options.text: A mind map
options.note: A mind map radiates themes from a central topic and does not sequence tasks or assign actors.

options.text: A context diagram
options.note: A context diagram shows the boundary of a system and the external entities that interact with it.

options.text: A use case diagram
options.note: A use case diagram shows the services actors need from a system, not the order of tasks.

options.text: A task scenario
options.note: A task scenario tells the story of one transaction rather than mapping a whole process.

questions.explanation: The visualisation list in Figure 5.1 includes process models, and the chapter describes them as flow charts of tasks, actors and flow that business stakeholders find accessible. A task scenario is the near miss because it also sets out steps, but it follows one transaction rather than mapping the whole process.

questions.stem: A workshop has finished generating ideas. The facilitator now asks each participant for their immediate reaction, intending to discard any idea that provokes strong dislike or no reaction at all. Which Six Hats perspective is this?

options.text: Green hat
options.note: The green hat is used to generate ideas, which the group has already done.

options.text: White hat
options.note: The white hat gathers the facts needed to judge an idea.

options.text: Yellow hat
options.note: The yellow hat looks for advantages and the forces that would make an idea succeed.

options.text: Black hat
options.note: The black hat looks for drawbacks and the forces militating against success.

options.text: Red hat
options.note: The red hat records emotional responses and treats strong dislike or indifference as grounds for removal.

options.text: Blue hat
options.note: The blue hat is the facilitator's perspective on running the workshop process.

questions.explanation: The red hat captures feelings rather than reasons, and the chapter says ideas that provoke strong dislike, or no reaction at all, become candidates for removal. The black hat is the near miss because it is also negative, but it is reasoned criticism of drawbacks rather than a gut reaction.

questions.stem: A sponsor asks for one workshop to redesign the whole order-to-cash process, from sales enquiry through to cash collection. What does the chapter say the facilitator should do with that objective?

options.text: Invite every stakeholder in the process and rely on break-out groups
options.note: Break-out groups help a large group contribute but do not make an oversized objective achievable in one session.

options.text: Split it into sub-objectives, each the basis of a separate session
options.note: A workshop objective must be achievable in the time available, so a large one is broken into sub-objectives.

options.text: Book a neutral venue away from the office
options.note: A neutral venue suits a contentious subject and does not reduce the scope of the objective.

options.text: Appoint a scribe and capture points on a flipchart
options.note: Scribing protects the facilitator's attention but leaves the objective unchanged.

options.text: Run the session as a two-day hothouse
options.note: A hothouse is an intense session for innovation and prototyping, not for redesigning an existing process.

options.text: Apply the Six Hats sequence to evaluate the options
options.note: Six Hats structures evaluation after ideas exist and does not make the objective achievable.

questions.explanation: The chapter's first preparation decision is the objective, and it must be achievable within the time constraints; a sizeable objective is split into sub-objectives, each forming the basis of an individual session. A hothouse is tempting because it is a long session, but it is aimed at innovation and prototyping rather than at scoping an existing process redesign.

questions.stem: An experienced underwriter processes a renewal without consulting any notes and cannot explain afterwards how she reached her decision. The analyst asks her to repeat the task while describing each step as she does it. Which technique is this?

options.text: Formal observation
options.note: Formal observation watches the task but does not require the performer to explain the reasoning behind each step.

options.text: Shadowing
options.note: Shadowing follows a role over days to learn what the job involves rather than capturing the reasoning in one task.

options.text: An ethnographic study
options.note: Ethnography is an extended study of the environment and culture over weeks or months.

options.text: Protocol analysis
options.note: Protocol analysis has staff perform a specified task while describing each step, which surfaces skills that cannot easily be put into words.

options.text: Activity sampling
options.note: Activity sampling records what people are doing at set intervals.

options.text: A structured interview
options.note: An interview away from the task would not capture the steps as they are performed.

questions.explanation: Protocol analysis is the performing and describing approach, likened in the chapter to training a new colleague or a learner driver being shown and told at the same time. Formal observation is the near miss because the analyst watches the same task, but nothing is described aloud.

questions.stem: An analyst observes a team on a Wednesday morning and reports that the month-end reconciliation is not carried out, because nobody performed it while she was there. What is wrong with her conclusion?

options.text: A single observation shows only what happens on that occasion
options.note: The chapter warns that one visit can miss routine tasks that are not performed daily.

options.text: The team was performing to the rulebook because they knew they were watched
options.note: That risk changes how a task is done, not whether it appears at all that morning.

options.text: She should have used protocol analysis to hear the steps described
options.note: Protocol analysis adds spoken explanation but would not reveal a task that did not occur.

options.text: Observation is only valid for physical work such as warehouse picking
options.note: Sedentary work is less suited to observation, but observation is still valid there.

options.text: She needed trade union approval before observing
options.note: Approval is a precondition in a unionised workplace, not the reason the task was missed.

options.text: She recorded opinions rather than facts
options.note: Observation produces factual data, and the flaw lies in the timing of the visit.

questions.explanation: Observation shows what happens on the day of the visit, so a weekly or monthly task can be missed entirely; watching the task several times is the chapter's remedy. Performing to the rulebook is the tempting alternative because it is a real caveat of observation, but it distorts how a task is done rather than hiding it.

questions.stem: A business analyst is new to a procurement department and will spend two days at the side of one experienced buyer, asking questions as the work unfolds, to learn what the role involves. Which approach is this?

options.text: Formal observation
options.note: Formal observation watches a specified task being performed and records its steps.

options.text: Protocol analysis
options.note: Protocol analysis requires the person to describe each step aloud while performing one specified task.

options.text: Shadowing
options.note: Shadowing follows one member of staff for a period of days to find out what the role entails.

options.text: An ethnographic study
options.note: Ethnography lasts weeks or months and studies the culture of a whole environment.

options.text: Activity sampling
options.note: Activity sampling records at intervals what each member of a group is doing.

options.text: A structured interview
options.note: An interview would not show the work as it happens or the knowledge that is never written down.

questions.explanation: Shadowing is following a member of staff for a period, such as one or two days, to understand a specific user role and pick up the aspects they take for granted. Protocol analysis is the near miss because it also involves explanation, but it is confined to one specified task rather than the whole role.

questions.stem: Interviews have produced a tidy description of a stores process, but the analyst suspects it omits steps that staff no longer notice they perform. Which technique best addresses that gap?

options.text: Document analysis
options.note: Procedure manuals tend to describe what the process was meant to be rather than current practice.

options.text: A survey of the stores team
options.note: A survey gathers opinions at a distance and would not reveal unnoticed steps.

options.text: A focus group with the stores team
options.note: A focus group elicits opinions, and the missing steps are not a matter of opinion.

options.text: Scenario analysis
options.note: Scenarios explore how a transaction might unfold rather than what staff currently do without thinking.

options.text: Activity sampling
options.note: Activity sampling records what people are doing at intervals but does not explain the detail of each step.

options.text: Observation
options.note: Watching the work as it happens surfaces the taken-for-granted knowledge that stakeholders do not think to mention.

questions.explanation: The chapter's advantage of observation is that it captures tacit knowledge, the things staff take for granted and so never think to report in an interview. Activity sampling is the near miss because it also involves watching, but it samples what people are doing rather than showing the detail of how a task is done.

questions.stem: An analyst is preparing to interview a clerk who processes customer refunds. Which line of questioning fits her level in the STOP hierarchy?

options.text: The terms of reference and alignment with corporate strategy
options.note: Those are strategic level concerns.

options.text: Source documents, bottlenecks and the workarounds she uses
options.note: The operational level covers the actual tasks, source documents, bottlenecks and workarounds.

options.text: CSFs, KPIs and the associated reporting requirements
options.note: Those belong to the tactical level.

options.text: The approach the investigation will take
options.note: The approach to the investigation is agreed at the strategic level.

options.text: Management information needs for the board
options.note: Management information needs are raised at the strategic level.

options.text: New business requirements that align tactics with strategy
options.note: Those are tactical level concerns.

questions.explanation: STOP places strategic, tactical and operational management in a hierarchy, and the operational level is about the tasks as performed, including source documents, bottlenecks and workarounds. Tactical is the near miss because a supervisor also discusses process, but tactical questions concern performance targets and management control rather than the task itself.

questions.stem: Three supervisors each estimate that their team handles about 200 calls a day, and the three figures are inconsistent. What does the chapter say the analyst should do?

options.text: Average the three figures and use that as the baseline
options.note: Averaging opinions does not make them accurate.

options.text: Interview a fourth supervisor to break the tie
options.note: More interviews produce more opinions rather than measurement.

options.text: Accept the most senior supervisor's figure
options.note: Seniority does not make an estimate accurate.

options.text: Ask the three supervisors to agree a figure between them
options.note: Agreement would produce a consensus of opinion, not a measured volume.

options.text: Re-interview each supervisor with a longer agenda
options.note: A longer interview still yields opinion rather than data.

options.text: Confirm the figures with a quantitative technique
options.note: Interview information is often opinion from one perspective, so volumes must be confirmed before firm conclusions.

questions.explanation: A stated disadvantage of interviews is that the information is often opinion based and seen from one perspective, so quantitative data may be needed to confirm it. Asking the supervisors to agree is the tempting option because it sounds like resolving the conflict, but it produces consensus rather than accuracy.

questions.stem: An interview is drawing to a close and the analyst wants the relationship to remain workable for later contact. What does the chapter recommend?

options.text: Summarise actions, explain next steps and agree further contact
options.note: The closure covers all three, and managing expectations keeps the door open with senior stakeholders.

options.text: Write up the notes at once and send them to the interviewee to confirm their accuracy
options.note: That is the follow-up stage after the interview, not the closure.

options.text: Send the agenda a few days beforehand so the interviewee can prepare
options.note: That happens before the interview takes place.

options.text: Ask for an overview of the interviewee's responsibilities
options.note: That opens the body of the interview.

options.text: Record the interview so that no notes need to be taken during the discussion
options.note: Recording is a decision taken during the interview and does not close it.

options.text: Confirm the terms of reference for the investigation
options.note: That belongs to a strategic level interview, not to every closure.

questions.explanation: The closure has three parts: summarise points, actions and timescales; explain what happens next; and ask how further contact should be made, which is what keeps the door open. Sending notes for confirmation is the near miss because it is also about the relationship, but it is the follow-up stage and happens after the interview.

questions.stem: A business analyst argues that interviews are worth the time because staff cooperate later only if they believe the analyst understands their concerns. Which interview advantage is she describing?

options.text: Obtaining quantitative data about volumes and frequencies
options.note: Quantitative data comes from surveys, activity sampling and records.

options.text: Reaching a consensus view across departments
options.note: Consensus is the aim of a workshop.

options.text: Capturing knowledge that staff cannot put into words
options.note: That is what observation and protocol analysis address.

options.text: Building a relationship with each stakeholder
options.note: The chapter says staff gain confidence when the analyst appreciates their concerns, which improves cooperation.

options.text: Demonstrating the look and feel of a proposed solution
options.note: That is prototyping.

options.text: Confirming that the requirements have been understood
options.note: Confirmation of requirements comes from prototyping or review, not from the relationship itself.

questions.explanation: One of the two main interview benefits is building a relationship, so that business staff believe the analyst understands their work and will not impose a solution that overlooks their needs. Capturing tacit knowledge is the near miss because it is also about understanding the work, but it is an advantage of observation rather than of the interview.

questions.stem: An analyst finishes a demanding interview at four in the afternoon and has two more the next morning. What does the chapter say about the notes?

options.text: Wait until all the interviews are finished so that the notes are consistent
options.note: Delay loses detail and the account cannot be confirmed while it is fresh.

options.text: Keep rough notes and interpret them during analysis
options.note: Rough notes taken under time pressure will be incomplete and unconfirmed.

options.text: Transcribe a recording instead, since it is more accurate
options.note: Transcription takes about an hour for ten minutes of recording, so it is not the answer to a tight schedule.

options.text: Send the notes to the interviewee's manager for approval
options.note: The interviewee confirms the accuracy of their own account.

options.text: File the notes without confirmation to save the interviewee's time
options.note: Unconfirmed notes are not agreed and cannot be relied on as project documentation.

options.text: Write them up by the next day and have the interviewee confirm them
options.note: Notes must be completed while fresh and approved by the interviewee before becoming project documentation.

questions.explanation: The chapter says to write up the notes as soon as possible and usually by the next day, then send them to the interviewee to confirm they are accurate. Transcribing is tempting as the more thorough option, but the chapter notes that an hour of transcription yields only ten minutes of interview.

questions.stem: An analyst writes down the sequence of steps for a customer order on the assumption that nothing goes wrong and every check passes. What is this sequence called?

options.text: An extension
options.note: An extension is an alternative path taken when a control condition is not met.

options.text: A control condition
options.note: A control condition is what must be true to move from one step to the next.

options.text: The main success scenario
options.note: It is also called the happy day scenario: the default path when there are no complications.

options.text: A precondition
options.note: A precondition is what must be true before the scenario begins.

options.text: A post-condition
options.note: A post-condition is what must be true once the scenario has concluded.

options.text: An exception situation
options.note: An exception situation is one that requires an alternative path.

questions.explanation: The first three steps of scenario development establish the default path, known as the main success scenario or happy day scenario. An extension is the near miss because it is also a path through the scenario, but it is the alternative taken when a control condition fails.

questions.stem: A business analyst has identified the task to be modelled and the sequence of steps it involves. According to the scenario development process, what comes next?

options.text: Define the control conditions for moving between steps
options.note: The process runs from task to steps to control conditions to exception situations.

options.text: Identify the exception situations that require alternative paths
options.note: Exceptions are identified after the control conditions are defined.

options.text: Define the preconditions and post-conditions of the scenario
options.note: These belong to the scenario description but are not the next step in the process.

options.text: Identify the business event that triggers the transaction
options.note: The trigger is part of identifying the task, which is already done.

options.text: Develop the test scripts from the scenario
options.note: Test scripts are a later benefit of a completed scenario.

options.text: Build a prototype from the scenario
options.note: Prototyping may follow a scenario but is not a step within it.

questions.explanation: Figure 5.4 orders the work as identify the task, identify the steps and sequence, define the control conditions, then identify exception situations. Exception situations is the near miss because it is the next step after this one, not the immediate next step.

questions.stem: A team is sure its procedure covers every case. The analyst walks through each step asking what must be true to continue and what might happen instead, and the team finds several gaps. Why does this work?

options.text: The analyst sees the work as it happens rather than relying on recall
options.note: That describes observation.

options.text: Each transition prompts the user to ask what else might be true
options.note: That questioning surfaces exceptions and tacit knowledge, which is the key strength of scenarios.

options.text: The group reaches a consensus view in a single session
options.note: Consensus is a workshop benefit and is not what makes the technique work.

options.text: The scenario gives a pictorial view of the whole business situation
options.note: That is the role of a rich picture.

options.text: The written description removes the need for interviews
options.note: Scenarios supplement other techniques rather than replacing them.

options.text: The scenario records the physical conditions in which the task is performed
options.note: Physical context comes from observation.

questions.explanation: Scenarios are a framework for discovering the exceptions that need alternative paths, because each transition between steps is a prompt to ask what else might be true. Observation is the tempting alternative because it also deals with what really happens, but it does not use structured questioning about each step.

questions.stem: A facilitator wants a group to find the exceptions that the analysts have missed. Which exercise does the chapter recommend?

options.text: Ask the group to brainstorm every possible exception to the process
options.note: Brainstorming generates threads but not the structured, step-by-step extensions this exercise produces.

options.text: Present the happy day scenario and ask the group to confirm it
options.note: Confirmation tests the default path rather than the gaps around it.

options.text: Ask each participant to write exceptions on sticky notes and group the notes afterwards
options.note: Affinity grouping organises known issues without forcing the group through an alternative path.

options.text: Ask break-out groups for a concrete scenario that breaks the happy day path
options.note: Experience shows this increases creativity and produces many valid extensions.

options.text: Apply the red hat to see which exceptions people feel strongly about
options.note: The red hat captures emotional response and does not generate exceptions.

options.text: Build a high fidelity prototype of the process instead
options.note: A prototype can be based on a scenario but does not itself discover exceptions.

questions.explanation: The chapter describes putting stakeholders into break-out groups with the instruction to produce a concrete scenario that does not conform to the happy day path, and says experience shows this increases creativity. Brainstorming is the near miss because it also generates possibilities, but it lacks the step-by-step structure that forces out the extensions.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to prototype the single order entry screen or the whole order process. Which prototyping decision are they making?

options.text: Fidelity
options.note: Fidelity is how closely the prototype resembles the final system, from paper sketch to simulated screens.

options.text: Functionality
options.note: Functionality is whether the prototype accesses and uses data.

options.text: Navigation
options.note: Navigation paths are what a prototype helps to assess, not the decision described here.

options.text: Usability
options.note: Usability requirements are elicited by demonstrating the prototype.

options.text: Scope
options.note: Scope is whether the prototype covers one screen or an entire system or process.

options.text: Accessibility
options.note: Accessibility requirements may be elicited by a prototype but are not the decision being made.

questions.explanation: The chapter names three decisions to settle before building: scope, fidelity and functionality. Fidelity is the near miss because it is the other decision that shapes how the prototype looks, but it concerns the level of detail rather than how much of the system is covered.

questions.stem: A designer produces a plain layout showing where the elements of a web page sit and how a user would move between them. It deliberately has no images, colours or graphics. What is this?

options.text: A wireframe
options.note: A wireframe shows layout and navigation and usually lacks images, colours and graphics.

options.text: A high fidelity prototype
options.note: A high fidelity prototype simulates how the finished screens will look.

options.text: A mock-up
options.note: A mock-up is built from flipcharts and sticky notes in a workshop to prototype screens or a process.

options.text: A storyboard
options.note: A storyboard presents a visual scenario rather than a page layout.

options.text: A rich picture
options.note: A rich picture is an unstructured view of a whole business situation.

options.text: A low fidelity prototype
options.note: A low fidelity prototype is a sketch or mock-up used to explore requirements, not a page layout convention.

questions.explanation: Wireframes are created primarily to show the layout of a screen, document or web page and how the elements and navigation might work, and they usually lack images, colours and graphics. A low fidelity prototype is the near miss because it is also rough, but the distinguishing feature here is the layout and navigation purpose, not the lack of detail.

questions.stem: A prototype runs on a stand-alone laptop with dummy records and responds instantly. The sponsor concludes that the solution is nearly ready for delivery. Which prototyping hazard is this?

options.text: The prototyping cycle spinning out of control
options.note: Endless iterations would show as delay and rework, not as a false impression of readiness.

options.text: Business staff assuming delivery is close because the purpose was not explained
options.note: That hazard concerns the purpose of the exercise rather than its performance.

options.text: The prototype being built at too low a fidelity
options.note: Low fidelity limits what can be learned but does not create an illusion of performance.

options.text: Requirements being validated too early in the lifecycle
options.note: Early validation is one of the advantages of prototyping.

options.text: The analyst using live operational data in a demonstration
options.note: Data choice is a functionality decision and is not the cause of the illusion.

options.text: Expectations raised by a prototype faster than the final system
options.note: A stand-alone machine with dummy data responds faster than a shared system, so real delays should be built in.

questions.explanation: The chapter warns that a stand-alone machine with dummy data will respond faster than a shared system used by thousands, so the prototype should include a realistic delay. Unexplained purpose is the near miss because it also creates a false impression of progress, but there the cause is the exercise not being introduced, not the machine's speed.

questions.stem: Business staff cannot say what they want from a new booking process, and every attempt to write requirements produces something different. Which prototyping approach does the chapter suggest?

options.text: A high fidelity prototype built in the development environment
options.note: High fidelity work suits confirming requirements that are already understood.

options.text: A low fidelity mock-up built in a workshop with sticky notes
options.note: Where staff are unclear, a minimal scope, low fidelity mock-up helps them visualise what is possible.

options.text: An evolutionary prototype released into live operation
options.note: Evolutionary prototyping delivers critical functionality in Agile delivery rather than exploring unclear needs.

options.text: A wireframe of the final screen layout
options.note: A wireframe assumes the screen layout is the question, when the process itself is unclear.

options.text: A prototype using live operational data
options.note: Live data is unnecessary and risky when the purpose is to explore possibilities.

options.text: A prototype covering the entire system
options.note: Prototypes for elicitation tend to be minimal in scope.

questions.explanation: Where business staff are unclear about their requirements, the chapter describes low fidelity prototypes with minimal scope, mocked up from flipcharts, whiteboards and sticky notes, often in a workshop. High fidelity software prototypes are the near miss because they are also prototypes, but they are used to analyse or confirm requirements that are already understood.

questions.stem: An analyst groups people so that every employee is covered by one group needing access to HR services and every customer by another needing product services. Which technique is this?

options.text: Stakeholder analysis
options.note: Stakeholder analysis identifies individuals and groups affected by a change, with their interests and influence.

options.text: Persona analysis
options.note: Personas are archetypes that supplement a user role rather than define the group that needs the services.

options.text: User role analysis
options.note: It identifies specific groups of individuals where all members need access to a particular set of services.

options.text: Scenario analysis
options.note: Scenarios describe tasks and transactions rather than groups needing services.

options.text: Use case modelling
options.note: Use cases describe what a system does for an actor, not how users are grouped by common access needs.

options.text: A rich picture
options.note: A rich picture records a situation pictorially rather than defining user groups.

questions.explanation: User role analysis defines generic titles such as customer, supplier and regulator, where every member of the group needs the same set of services from the business system. Stakeholder analysis is the near miss because it also groups people, but it maps interest and influence rather than common access needs.

questions.stem: The team has defined a single customer user role and cannot decide which features matter, because customers differ so much. Which technique overcomes this?

options.text: Splitting the customer role into more generic user roles
options.note: More generic labels still cover wide groups and add no human detail.

options.text: Stakeholder analysis
options.note: Stakeholder analysis maps interests and influence rather than the variety of customer needs.

options.text: A survey of customers
options.note: A survey collects data at scale but does not create the archetypes used in design.

options.text: Persona analysis
options.note: Personas are archetypes of real customers that show why different people use the service.

options.text: Scenario analysis
options.note: Scenarios describe transactions rather than the characteristics of the people involved.

options.text: A focus group of customers
options.note: A focus group gathers opinions and does not by itself produce archetypes.

questions.explanation: The stated disadvantage of a generic user role is that it covers too wide a group to envisage how individuals will use the system, and persona analysis is the supplementary technique that overcomes it. Splitting the role is the near miss because it also addresses breadth, but more generic labels do not add the characteristics that make the difference visible.

questions.stem: A team designing an online service defines an archetypal user with a specific disability so that the accessibility requirements can be explored fully. What have they created?

options.text: A user role
options.note: A user role is a generic group such as customer or supplier, not a character with characteristics.

options.text: An actor
options.note: An actor is defined by what it does in a use case rather than who it is.

options.text: A stakeholder
options.note: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in the change.

options.text: A scenario
options.note: A scenario is the story of a task or transaction.

options.text: A prototype
options.note: A prototype is a simulation of a system or process.

options.text: A persona
options.note: A persona is an archetype representing a group of users, used here to explore accessibility requirements.

questions.explanation: Personas are archetypes that help the team envisage why and how different people use the service, and the chapter gives a persona with a specific disability as the way to explore accessibility requirements fully. A user role is the near miss because it is also a way of grouping users, but it is a generic title rather than a character with characteristics.

questions.stem: A questionnaire asks for the respondent's age band, gender and length of service, so that responses can be analysed by staff group. Which section of the survey is this?

options.text: The heading section
options.note: The heading explains the purpose, use of the data and any incentive.

options.text: The classification section
options.note: It captures respondent details used to categorise responses by pre-defined analysis criteria.

options.text: The data section
options.note: The data section holds the main body of questions.

options.text: The introduction
options.note: The three-part structure is heading, classification and data, with no separate introduction.

options.text: The sampling section
options.note: Sampling is a design consideration, not one of the three sections.

options.text: The analysis section
options.note: Analysis happens after the survey closes rather than inside it.

questions.explanation: The classification section captures details about the respondent and provides the basis for categorising responses by criteria such as age, gender or length of service. The data section is the near miss because it holds the questions, but the questions there are about the subject of the survey rather than about the respondent.

questions.stem: A survey asks how often a respondent uses the service, offering daily, weekly, monthly and occasionally. Several respondents could tick more than one box, and some patterns of use are not covered. Which principle has been broken?

options.text: The Likert scale convention, which fixes the number of points on an agreement scale
options.note: A Likert scale is an agreement scale of five or seven points, not the issue here.
