questions.explanation: The distinction is about what the requirement belongs to: the business side covers policy, standards and technical infrastructure constraints, while the solution side covers the features and the level of service those features must provide.

questions.stem: 'The organisation must comply with data protection legislation.' Which type of requirement is this?

options.text: A general business requirement
options.note: General requirements define business policies, standards and compliance areas, and are broad enough to be decomposed.

options.text: A technical business requirement
options.note: Technical requirements cover hardware, software, interoperability and internet policy.

options.text: A functional solution requirement
options.note: Functional requirements state features the solution must provide.

options.text: A non-functional solution requirement
options.note: Non-functional requirements state levels of service such as performance and security.

options.text: A business rule constraint
options.note: Business rules govern decisions within a requirement, not the legislative obligation itself.

options.text: A transition requirement
options.note: Transition requirements concern migration, communication and release.

questions.explanation: The giveaway is breadth. A statement that the organisation must comply with legislation cannot be delivered by a feature, so it gets decomposed into functional and non-functional requirements such as recording, accessing and archiving data.

questions.stem: 'Only the current and previous two major versions of the supported web browsers are permitted.' Which type of requirement is this?

options.text: A technical business requirement, covering the technical policies that apply across the organisation
options.note: Technical requirements cover hardware, software, interoperability and internet policy, and apply to all change projects.

options.text: A general business requirement, covering branding and culture
options.note: Branding and culture are general sub-categories.

options.text: A functional solution requirement
options.note: This is a constraint on technology, not a feature.

options.text: A non-functional solution requirement
options.note: It constrains the platform rather than setting a level of service.

options.text: A legal requirement
options.note: No legislation is involved.

options.text: A user interface requirement
options.note: Interface requirements concern look and feel and interaction.

questions.explanation: Technical requirements are the organisation-wide policies about technology, and they bind every project rather than one solution. The internet sub-category is exactly where supported browser policies sit.

questions.stem: Which pairing of examples is correct for functional and non-functional requirements?

options.text: Functional is the ability to place an order; non-functional is that the order must complete within eight seconds
options.note: Features are functional and levels of service are non-functional.

options.text: Functional is that the system is available 24/7; non-functional is the ability to place an order
options.note: These are the wrong way round.

options.text: Functional is security; non-functional is data entry
options.note: Security and data entry are both non-functional categories.

options.text: Functional is usability; non-functional is reporting
options.note: Usability is non-functional.

options.text: Functional is capacity; non-functional is processing an order
options.note: Capacity is non-functional.

options.text: They are the same type expressed at different levels of detail
options.note: They answer different questions: what it does, and how well it must do it.

questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe what the solution provides, typically data entry, processing and reporting. Non-functional requirements describe the level of service in areas like performance, security, availability and usability.

questions.stem: A usability requirement asks how easy it is to remember how to use a system after not using it for a while. Which of Nielsen's five usability dimensions is that?

options.text: Memorability
options.note: Nielsen's dimensions are learnability, efficiency, memorability, satisfaction and errors.

options.text: Learnability, which concerns how easy the system is to learn from new
options.note: Learning and remembering are separate dimensions.

options.text: Efficiency, which concerns how quickly tasks are completed
options.note: Efficiency is about speed of use.

options.text: Satisfaction, which concerns whether it is pleasant to use
options.note: Satisfaction is about the experience rather than recall.

options.text: Error, which concerns how likely mistakes are
options.note: Error is about mistakes.

options.text: Accessibility, which concerns disability
options.note: Accessibility is a related but separate non-functional area.

questions.explanation: The five dimensions are easy to blur, and the exam asks about them directly. Memorability is specifically about returning to the system after a gap, which is why it can be tested differently from learnability.

questions.stem: Which four disability categories does the chapter give for accessibility requirements?

options.text: Cognitive, physical or motor, hearing, and visual
options.note: Those are the four aspects to consider.

options.text: Temporary, permanent, situational and progressive
options.note: These are accessibility situations rather than the chapter's categories.

options.text: Motor, sensory, mental and social
options.note: Only motor appears among the chapter's four.

options.text: Visual, auditory, speech and learning
options.note: Speech and learning are not among the four.

options.text: Physical, emotional, intellectual and social
options.note: None of these four appears in that form.

options.text: Congenital, acquired, age-related and injury-related
options.note: These describe causes rather than categories of disability.

questions.explanation: Accessibility requirements exist to enable access for people who might otherwise be excluded, and the chapter narrows it to those four. The remedies it gives are varied, including assistive technology, images and physical facilities such as ramps.

questions.stem: A stakeholder says a transaction 'must be done quickly'. What does the chapter require instead?

options.text: A precise, testable statement, optionally with a minimum time and a maximum acceptable time
options.note: The chapter rejects vague wording and shows the eight second minimum with a fifteen second maximum under load.

options.text: A qualitative statement, because performance varies with load
options.note: Variation is handled by stating both a normal and a peak figure.

options.text: A statement of the business benefit of speed
options.note: Benefit explains why, but does not make the requirement testable.

options.text: A technical design decision about server capacity
options.note: Design follows the requirement.

options.text: A note that speed will be confirmed during acceptance testing
options.note: Deferring the definition is the failure the chapter warns about.

options.text: A relative statement compared with the current system
options.note: Relative wording still cannot be tested.

questions.explanation: Performance is the category where vagueness is most damaging, because nobody can test 'quickly'. Stating a normal target and a degraded peak target is the pattern the chapter recommends.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter say requirements should be arranged in a hierarchy?

options.text: To trace requirements back to the business driver so they stay aligned with objectives and strategy
options.note: The hierarchy links functional and non-functional requirements back to general and technical ones.

options.text: To decide which requirements to build first
options.note: Prioritisation is a separate activity with its own techniques.

options.text: To allocate requirements to developers
options.note: Allocation is planning work, not the purpose of the hierarchy.

options.text: To reduce the number of requirements
options.note: The hierarchy does not remove any requirement.

options.text: To convert functional requirements into non-functional ones
options.note: The categories remain distinct.

options.text: To replace the need for validation
options.note: Validation is still required.

questions.explanation: The hierarchy is a traceability device. It shows why a requirement exists, which supports prioritisation, deciding when to deliver, judging whether a requirement can be dropped, and understanding the impact of a change request.

questions.stem: Which relationship between functional and non-functional requirements does the chapter describe?

options.text: Some functional requirements have related non-functional requirements, and some non-functional requirements apply to several functional requirements
options.note: The chapter states both directions.

options.text: Every functional requirement needs exactly one non-functional requirement
options.note: The relationship is not one to one.

options.text: Non-functional requirements never relate to functional ones
options.note: The hierarchy explicitly connects them.

options.text: Functional requirements are always derived from other functional requirements
options.note: Derivation runs from general and technical requirements.

options.text: Non-functional requirements sit above general requirements in the hierarchy
options.note: General and technical requirements are the broad ones at the top.

options.text: The two are alternatives chosen according to project type
options.note: Both are needed.

questions.explanation: Many to many is the practical shape, which is why a requirements catalogue records associated non-functional requirements per entry rather than assuming a pairing.

questions.stem: What does the chapter say requirements are driven by, if they are not to be merely ideas or opinions?

options.text: The organisation's values, strategy, objectives and performance measures
options.note: That is the basis the hierarchy traces up to.

options.text: The preferences of the most senior stakeholder
options.note: Opinion is exactly what the hierarchy is meant to expose.

options.text: The capabilities of the chosen technology platform
options.note: Technology constrains but does not justify a requirement.

options.text: The available project budget
options.note: Budget limits scope rather than defining need.

options.text: The number of stakeholders requesting the feature
options.note: Popularity is not the same as alignment.

options.text: The current system's functionality
options.note: Existing functionality is a starting point, not a driver.

questions.explanation: The chapter's test of a requirement is whether it supports a business objective; if it does not, it is questionable whether it is required at all. Tracing upward is how you find out.

questions.stem: A stakeholder says she cannot explain how she decides when a claim looks suspicious; she just knows. What kind of knowledge is this, and what does the chapter call it?

options.text: Tacit knowledge, summarised as knowing more than we can tell
options.note: The chapter uses Polanyi's maxim and describes this as the unknown knowns.

options.text: Explicit knowledge, because she can describe her work
options.note: Explicit knowledge is what a stakeholder can readily identify and articulate.

options.text: Taken-for-granted information, because she assumes the analyst knows it
options.note: That is a related but distinct problem about unmentioned detail.

options.text: Front story, because she is presenting her work favourably
options.note: Front story is about describing practice more positively than it is.

options.text: Conceptual knowledge, because no process exists yet
options.note: Conceptual difficulty arises in new areas with no existing process.

options.text: Intuitive knowledge, which falls outside elicitation
options.note: Intuitive judgement is a form of tacit knowledge that can be explored.

questions.explanation: The clue is the inability to articulate, not reluctance. Tacit knowledge is the category the whole elicitation technique set exists to address, which is why observation, protocol analysis and prototyping appear in the toolkit.

questions.stem: An analyst asks an experienced operator to perform a task in discrete steps, talking through each step aloud, and to repeat this two or three times. Which technique is this?

options.text: Protocol analysis, used to surface unconscious skill
options.note: The chapter describes protocol analysis in those terms and notes it is how skills are often taught.

options.text: Shadowing, used to observe work as it happens
options.note: Shadowing watches without the talk-aloud step and repetition.

options.text: Activity sampling, used to record what happens at intervals
options.note: Sampling is quantitative observation.

options.text: Document analysis, used to read existing records
options.note: No documents are involved.

options.text: Scenario analysis, used to walk through possible futures
options.note: Scenario analysis explores situations rather than step-by-step task performance.

options.text: Storytelling, used to capture experience
options.note: Storytelling collects narratives rather than decomposing a task.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature is the verbalised, repeated walk-through. Skill performed automatically is invisible even to the person doing it, so making them stop and narrate is what turns it into something documentable.

questions.stem: During interviews, business staff describe current practice as far smoother than it is, because the analyst is seen as representing management. What is this called, and what is the remedy?

options.text: A favourable front story, which can be overcome by building relationships through interviews, observation or shadowing
options.note: The chapter names front story and back story and gives those approaches.

options.text: A tacit assumption, which is resolved by a longer interview
options.note: Tacit assumptions are about unexamined beliefs, not a presentational slant.

options.text: Conceptual difficulty, which is resolved by a prototype
options.note: Conceptual difficulty arises in unfamiliar business areas.

options.text: Organisational culture, which is resolved by escalation to the sponsor
options.note: Culture describes norms rather than this specific behaviour.

options.text: The unknown knowns, which are resolved by a workshop
options.note: Unknown knowns are knowledge the stakeholder cannot articulate.

options.text: A requirements conflict, which is resolved by the product owner
options.note: No conflict between requirements is being described.

questions.explanation: Front story is explicit knowledge distorted by who the analyst appears to represent. The remedy is trust and first-hand evidence, which is why observation and shadowing are named alongside interviewing.

questions.stem: Which three approaches does the chapter give for uncovering tacit knowledge, moving it towards explicit knowledge?

options.text: Observe, recount and enact
options.note: Observation and shadowing for observe, storytelling and scenario analysis for recount, prototyping and role play for enact.

options.text: Interview, document and model
options.note: Interviewing and document analysis are explicit-knowledge techniques.

options.text: Capture, prioritise and validate
options.note: These are framework activities, not tacit-knowledge approaches.

options.text: Ask, listen and record
options.note: Too general, and all slant towards explicit knowledge.

options.text: Prototype, test and release
options.note: These are delivery activities.

options.text: Survey, sample and analyse
options.note: These are quantitative investigation techniques.

questions.explanation: The three approaches map to different routes into knowledge: watching it, hearing it told, and acting it out. The chapter pairs each with specific techniques, which is the part worth remembering.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter recommend using a workshop to start requirements elicitation?

options.text: Because it draws requirements out from participants using discovery and visualisation techniques, and can resolve conflicts and evaluate prototypes
options.note: The chapter lists those uses for a facilitated workshop.

options.text: Because it removes the need for individual interviews
options.note: Interviews remain useful for overview requirements from managers.

options.text: Because workshops produce a complete requirements specification
options.note: Documentation is a later, separate activity.

options.text: Because workshops replace document analysis
options.note: Existing documents are still analysed.

options.text: Because workshops are the only technique that works in Agile
options.note: Several techniques apply.

options.text: Because workshops avoid the need for validation
options.note: Validation is still required.

questions.explanation: A workshop is the natural place to begin because it combines several techniques and several perspectives at once. The chapter is specific about what the facilitator does inside it: visualise, model, analyse critical success factors, walk through scenarios and test prototypes.

questions.stem: A requirement reads: 'As a receptionist I want to record, amend or cancel a booking.' Which filter applies?

options.text: Unravelling multiple requirements, because the statement contains three atomic requirements with different priorities and acceptance criteria
options.note: That is the chapter's own example of a multiple requirement.

options.text: Removing conflicts, because the three actions compete
options.note: They do not contradict one another.

options.text: Checking for solutions, because the statement names a screen
options.note: No solution is prescribed.

options.text: Confirming relevance, because cancellation may not be needed
options.note: Relevance is a different filter.

options.text: Confirming quality of expression, because the wording is verbose
options.note: The problem is plurality, not verbosity.

options.text: Evaluating feasibility, because three features may be unaffordable
options.note: Cost is not the defect described.

questions.explanation: One statement covering three actions cannot carry one priority or one set of acceptance criteria. Splitting into atomic requirements is what makes prioritisation, testing and delivery possible.

questions.stem: In MoSCoW, a requirement is essential to the solution but may be deferred to the second increment. Which priority is that?

options.text: Should have
options.note: Should have requirements are mandatory for the solution but may be deferred in the short term.

options.text: Must have
options.note: Must have requirements cannot be deferred without making the current increment unacceptable.

options.text: Could have
options.note: Could have requirements are desirable and may be excluded on timescale or budget grounds.

options.text: Want to have, but won't have this time
options.note: Those are deferred beyond the current plan altogether.

options.text: Nice to have
options.note: That is a different scheme's label rather than a MoSCoW level.

options.text: Mandatory
options.note: Mandatory is a general label, not one of the four MoSCoW shades.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature of should have is deferrable while still mandatory overall. Must have cannot slip at all; could have can be dropped and still leave an acceptable solution.

questions.stem: A car rental rule states that a person aged under 21 may not hire a car. Which category of business rule is that?

options.text: A constraint, which governs what may or may not be done
options.note: Constraints govern what is permitted, and the chapter gives under 21 car hire as its example.

options.text: Operational guidance, which governs how a decision is made
options.note: Operational guidance covers decisions, calculations and handling steps.

options.text: A functional requirement
options.note: The rule constrains behaviour rather than describing a feature.

options.text: A non-functional requirement
options.note: No level of service is being set.

options.text: A business policy standard from the general requirements
options.note: It may derive from policy, but as a rule it is a constraint.

options.text: A decision condition, which is a sub-category of operational guidance
options.note: Decision conditions are operational guidance, not constraints.

questions.explanation: The two business rule categories are constraints and operational guidance. Constraints set what is allowed; operational guidance sets how a transaction, decision or calculation is carried out.
